  The remuneration of mental health professionals h ave been revised in the programme and with effectiv e monitoring

current capacity after implementation of the scheme in 11 centres of excellence and 120 PG departments in mental health during

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
  The Committee is happy to note that some concrete  steps have been initiated by the Department for much-awaited 
revamping and augmentation of the National Mental H ealth Programme. These initiatives need to be const antly

Recommendations/observations  
15.11   The Committee notes with displeasure that t hough the Department has proposed to include 200 mo re districts 
under this component during the Eleventh Plan, fina l approval is yet to be given by the competent auth ority. The Committee is

  The department had proposed for expansion of DMHP  to 200 new districts. However, the EFC did not agr ee to the

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
  The main objective of the Programme has been to e nsure the availability and accessibility of minimum  mental 
healthcare for those suffering with mental illness,  particularly to the most vulnerable and underprivi leged sections 
amongst them. The Department would be failing in it s duty if it does not expand the Programme in a big  way so as to 
reach the remotest corners of the country. The Depa rtment cannot shy away from this social responsibil ity. Funds for 
the Programme have been ceremoniously revised downw ards at the RE stage owing to poor implementation s tatus. 
Department’s reply that the EFC did not agree to its proposal for expansion of DMHP to 200 new districts in view of the 
paucity of funds does not sound logical. The Department appears to have not presented its case based on sound logic and 
facts or it might not have inspired confidence of a ctually being able to execute the expansion work ba sed on its track-
record. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the  Department to focus on better utilization of the a llocated funds 
and effective implementation of the Programme. The Committee is sanguine that more efficient use of th e allocated 
funds would bolster the Department’s proposal for expansion of DMHP.

of NCCP to Rs.731.52 crore for the remaining two ye ars of the Eleventh Plan. The Committee hopes that this 
curtailment is not as a result of sub-optimal utili zation of the allocated funds due to poor implement ation of the 
Programme and wonders as to whether the Department has drawn an effective strategy to utilise even thi s curtailed 
amount fully in the remaining two years. The Commit tee would like to be apprised of the status and com ponents of the 
revised Programme and the details of the “concerted  plan of action to implement the revised programme on a priority 
basis”.

16.9   In order to identify weak links and ensure e ffective implementation of various components of th e programme, the

XVIII. MEDICAL EDUCATION  
18.2  The Committee is concerned with the fact that  as many as 10 colleges are being considered for wi thdrawal of recognition 
and 15 more being issued show cause notices. From t he large number of colleges caught compromising the  standards while 
being scrutinized, it is clear that all is not well . This clubbed with the fact that these colleges ar e those which have come under 
scheduled scrutiny and there may be many which keep  on functioning until they come under inspection sc rutiny, makes the 
matter more serious. The Committee would like to ha ve a brief about the status of inspection of all th e medical colleges inter-
alia  containing the selection procedure vide  which the colleges are selected for inspection, th e date of establishment of college, 
date of inspections, shortcomings noticed and actio n taken during the last 5 years. The Committee may also be informed of the 
details w. r. t. the progress made for withdrawal o f recognition of 10 colleges, show cause notice to 15 colleges and the court 
cases in respect of the 4 colleges.  
Action Taken  
  Procedure for conducting the inspection by the Medi cal Council of India  Presently, there are about 300 medical 
colleges in the country out of which 229 medical co lleges are recognized and remaining 71 medical coll eges have been 
approved for running MBBS courses and will be consi dered for recognition as per the provisions of Medi cal Council of India 
(MCI) regulations. 
  MCI carries out periodic inspections of medical c olleges as per the provisions of IMC Act and regula tions made 
thereunder. MCI conducted the inspections of medical colleges under section 10A, 11 (2) and 19 of IMC Act for establishment 
of new medical college, renewal of permission, reco gnition of medical colleges and continuance of reco gnition for award of 
MBBS degree. 
  The medical colleges are inspected by the MCI fro m time to time under the following categories: 
(i) The recognition of a medical college is reviewe d after every five years.  
(ii)  The permission of the approved medical colleg es is renewed every year till such time the medical  college is 
recognized. The permission is renewed if it is found during inspection that all the facilities are as per MCI norms. 
(iii)  Those medical colleges which apply for postg raduate courses for the first time after its recognition, are inspected. 
(iv)  A medical college is inspected when there is a complaint with regard to the malpractice for teaching faculty, clinical 
material and infrastructural facilities. 
(v)  Inspection of a medical college is also conduc ted on the direction of High Courts/Supreme Court. 
  After conducting the inspections under the above said provisions of IMC Act, MCI has so far recommended to the Central 
Government for withdrawal of recognition of 10 medi cal colleges and has issued show cause notice to 15  medical colleges in 
the country. A statement showing the present status of above 25 colleges is at Annexure-XI  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee had called for a status note in res pect of all the colleges inspected by the MCI durin g the last 5 
years inter-alia  containing - the selection procedure vide  which the colleges were selected for inspection, t he date of 
establishment of college, date of inspection(s), sh ortcomings noticed and action taken after such insp ection. The 
Committee is dismayed at the fact that the required information is conspicuously missing in the Action Taken Note. The 
Committee would accordingly like the Department to furnish the requisite information at the earliest.

19.4  The Committee notes with serious concern that  apart from marginal improvement in GDMO sub-cadre,  that too far too

cadres inspite of the sanctioned strength increasing in the three sub-cadres other than GDMO. The Comm ittee is not convinced 
with the Department’s efforts because had the Depar tment made sincere efforts there would have been so me kind of forward 
movement in filling up the vacancies over the years . The Committee cannot make out the delay in making  recruitments by 
UPSC. Promotion vacancies can be filled up by conve ning DPCs. Further, the Committee is unable to unde rstand the delay in 
notifying the revised CHS rules especially when the re is urgency involved in the matter. Temporary and  contractual measures 
can never be a solution in the long run. 
19.5   The Committee would like to be apprised abou t the details of contractual/temporary appointments made under CHS 
for the past one year. The Committee would also like to be furnished with a detailed note in respect of the posts under each sub-
cadre, inter-alia  covering issues like when it approached the UPSC f or making direct recruitments, holding of DPCs, rea sons 
for delay in notifying CHS rules and the efforts made by the Department for early filling up of the vacancies. 
Action Taken  
  Central Health Service is comprised of 4 sub-cadr es namely (i) Teaching; (ii) Non- Teaching; (iii) Public Health; and (iv) 
General Duty Medical Officers. First 3 sub-cadres a re specialist sub-cadres and recruitment in these s ub-cadres are made 
through UPSC by holding Interviews. On the other ha nd, recruitment in GDMO sub-cadre is made through C ombined Medical 
Service Examination conducted every year by the UPSC. The UPSC being a Constitutional Authority follow its own procedure 
and the Ministry has no role in recruitment process  except to make a request to Commission for expedit ing the process of 
recruitment that too in case of recruitment of spec ialists only. UPSC has a fixed schedule for conduct ing examination followed 
by interviews in case of GDMOs. It takes about one and quarter year for completing the recruitment process commencing from 
conducting of written examination to issue of offer s of appointment to the successful candidates. Ther e is no short cut to this 
method of recruitment of GDMOs. Moreover, most of t he selected candidates have been found to be pursui ng Post Graduate 
Courses and they do not join the posts till their PG course is completed. As such joining rate in GDMO sub-cadre is about 25-30 
% thereby causing the continuance of vacancies. 
  Further, since the appointment process takes long  time, the appointments are made on contractual bas is to ensure that the

21.5   The Committee takes note of a recent Delhi H igh Court directive given on 23rd March, 2007 where by private 
hospitals which were allotted cheap or free land by Government agencies are required to provide free treatment to poor patients 
at the rate of 10% in the Indoor Patient Department  (IPD) and 25% in the Outdoor Patient Department (O PD) of their total

provide 10% of the total beds free for poor (whose family income is Rs.4, 000/- or less per month) and free treatment to 25% of 
total patients free in the OPD in pursuance of Hon’ ble High Court orders dated 22.3.2007 and 17.7.2007 . Three hospitals 
namely, Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute, St. Stephens  Hospital and Mool Chand Khairati Ram Hospital are not providing free 

treatment stating that they are not covered under H igh Court orders. Ten other hospitals having 171 be ds have approached 
Hon’ble Supreme Court against the orders of Hon’ble High Court and have got interim stay with regard to providing free X-ray, 
CT Scan, Diagnostics etc. However, they are providi ng free treatment as in accordance with orders of H on’ble Supreme Court. 
Remaining 25 hospitals are providing free treatment  as per direction of Hon’ble Supreme Court. The Com mittee may be 
informed about the progress w.r.t.  the case filed by ten hospitals in Hon’ble Supreme Court. 
Action Taken  
  The matter is still sub-judice  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee is aware that the matter is still sub-judice . However, the Committee recommends to the 
Department to pursue the pending matter in the cour t vigorously so that it does not remain entangled i n prolonged 
litigation and the poor patients are deprived of mu ch needed healthcare needs. The Committee would app reciate if the 
present status of the case is submitted to it alongwith steps taken by the Department to expedite its early resolution. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
21.7   The Committee is pained by the fact that the  poor patients have to pay for the branded name of the medicines. This 
state of affairs is leading the poor patients to hu ge financial debts. Besides, procurement of the bra nded/generic branded 
medicines for Government hospitals, dispensaries an d CGHS leads to heavy burden on the Exchequer compr ising of precious 
taxpayer’s money. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to make it mandatory for the Gov ernment hospitals 
and CGHS to procure only generic medicines so that their procurement cost is reduced substantially wit hout compromising on 
the quality and efficacy of such medicines. The Com mittee further recommends the Department to initiat e some measures so 
that generic medicines are not marketed and sold as  generic branded medicines leading to exorbitant pr ices by the profiteering 
companies so that such medicines are available to the common man at reasonable prices. The Committee also recommends that 
it should be made mandatory for the Government doctors to prescribe only generic medicines. The Committee may be informed 
of the action taken by the Department in this regard. 
Action Taken 
  Branded Medicine, Generic Medicine, Branded Gener ic Medicines - The Committee has recommended that the use of 
generics in the public as well as private sectors w ill reduce the drug costs and increase drug availab ility. Competitive bulk 
procurement in generic name will help in procuring drugs at competitive prices. 
  It may be stated that earlier the Drugs and Cosme tics Rules, 1945 were amended vide  GSR 27(E) dated 17.01.1981 and 
the following Rule was inserted under rule 96 on labelling of drugs: 
  "The following preparations shall be labelled onl y with proper name of the drug and not with any trade name: 
(1) preparations containing any new drug as the sin gle active ingredient and approved under Rule 30-A,  69-B or 75-B 
by the Licensing Authority subject to the condition that such preparations should be marketed under a generic name 
only. 
(2) Preparations containing any drug specified in S chedule W as the single active ingredient." 
  At that time there were five drugs namely Analgin , Aspirin and its salts, Chlorpromazine and its sal ts, Ferrous Sulphate 
and Pipeprazine and its salts in Schedule W which w ere required to be marketed under generic names onl y. M/s. Heochst 
Pharmaceuticals filed a petition in the High Court challenging the above rule and Schedule W. The prov ision permiting the 
marketing of the five drugs in Schedule W only if l abelled only with the generic name was struck down by the High Court as 
arbitrary. High Court also directed to amend the no tification, with liberty to require the manufacture rs to prominently display, 
apart from the trade name of the drug, its generic name on the labels, containers or bottles (Union of  India v. Hoechst 
Pharmaceuticals Ltd., 1999 SCC (Cri) 138. 

  In compliance to the directions of the Court, the  said rule and Schedule W was omitted by the Minist ry of Health and 
Family Welfare vide  notification GSR 94(E) dated 08.02.2000. 
  At present there is no provision under Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules which makes it mandatory th at medicines 
should be marketed under generic name only without any brand name. Manufacturer or importer is free to  market their product 
either under a generic name only or under a brand name. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
  The Committee recommends to the Department to ini tiate suitable action to amend the Drugs and Cosmet ics Act 
and Rules so that generic medicines are not allowed  to be sold as branded medicines for the sake of pr ofiteering. The 
Committee would also recommend to the Department to  ensure availability of generic medicines in the op en market. 
The Committee would like to be informed about the action taken by the Department in this regard.  
Recommendations/Observations

Rajasthan which gives healthcare coverage to depriv ed sections of the society. The Committee feels tha t such welfare schemes 
should be encouraged in all possible ways including extending central funding for the same. The Committee may be apprised of

  Health being ‘State’ subject, it is the prerogati ve of respective State Government to take initiatives as per the needs of that 
State and availability of resources. In so far as M /O Health and Family Welfare is concerned, no propo sal is presently under 
consideration for providing central funding for State-specific Schemes. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  While appreciating a scheme for the healthcare cove rage for the deprived sections of the society by th e State of 
Rajasthan, the Committee had called for encouraging  such initiatives in different States in all possib le ways including 
extending central funding for the same. The Departm ent’s cold response to this suggestion by terming “ health” as a 
State subject and stating that there was no proposa l for providing central funding for the State-speci fic subjects is 
nothing but outrightly rejecting a good initiative on technical grounds. Had the Department been serio us on this

II.  BUDGETARY PROVISION 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.4   The Committee views with serious concern the trend of allocation of funds and utilization thereo f in some other crucial 
programmes such as National Programme for Control o f Blindness, Iodine Deficiency Disorder Control Pro gramme, 
Procurement of Drugs and Equipments under RCH, Information Education and Communication (Both RCH and Non-RCH) and

far from satisfactory. The Committee has been repea tedly cautioning the Department to take remedial me asures to ensure 
optimum utilization of funds year after year. Howev er, no significant improvement has been noticed so far. The case for 
Procurement of Drugs and Equipments under RCH remai ns a classic example, where, during 2008-09 Rs.300 crore were 
allocated and no expenditure was made. Again, in 20 09-10 an initial outlay of Rs.1 00 crore were made under the same head 
which was revised upwards to Rs.150 crore and no expenditure is reported to be there up till January, 2010. Approved outlay of 
Rs.1500 crore for the Eleventh Plan has thus remained unspent in spite of three years of the Plan period being over. 
Action Taken  
  Under the scheme Procurement of Drug and Equipmen ts under RCH, RE (2009-10) was Rs.150 crores and as  per the 
status of expenditure as on 31.3.2010, the funds under the scheme stand fully utilized. However, during 2008-09, no funds could 
be utilized against BE of Rs.300 crores due to non-finalisation of MOU with World Bank. As desired by the Committee, sincere 
efforts will continue to be made by the Ministry to  ensure optimum and judicious utilization of funds under each and every 
scheme. 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.5   The Committee strongly feel that poor plannin g and execution on the part of the Department regar ding the various on-
going schemes have been responsible for such a disc ouraging scenario. The Committee is well aware of t he fact that in a vast 

country like ours, with healthcare facilities espec ially in the rural areas showing a negligible prese nce, need for additional fund 
will also be there. The Committee has also been str ongly advocating the case for enhanced allocation o f funds for NRHM but 
the trend of under-utilization/unutilisation weakens the justification for higher provision of funds. The Committee is also aware 
of the fact that Union Government alone cannot achieve the targeted goals. It has to carry out the implementation with the active 
support of State Governments. The Committee, theref ore, once again recommends the Department to make i ts monitoring 
mechanism more effective so that such large amount of funds do not lapse/remain unutilized. The Commit tee also suggests the 
Department to undertake a comprehensive self-assess ment study on the means and methods used to improve  financial 
accountability under the Mission so far, and based on the findings, to devise a mechanism whereby funds utilization for the rest 
of the Mission period could be in a better state. T aking note of significant and persistent shortfall in utilization of the budgeted 
funds, the Committee would like the Department to e xercise greater prudence in their budget formulatio n and make their 
estimates only after proper assessment and planning. 
Action Taken  
  The Ministry has put into place a comprehensive, multi projected strategy for regular monitoring, co ncurrent evaluation 
and local feedback with respect to various components of the schemes. Monthly review meeting on expenditure are being taken 
by Secretary. (H&FW) with senior level officers. Pe riodic review meeting are also taken by Secretary w ith State Health 
Secretaries and Mission Directors of the States.

the Ministry to oversee the release of funds, monit oring of Utilisation Certificates and Audit Reports . The increased focus on

the number of financial transactions in the sector is expected to increase substantially in the coming  years, the NRHM has 
envisaged augmentation of accounting manpower at th e level of the PHCs in all States. The State Progra mme Management 
Units (PMUs) have also been advised to constitute F MGs within the PMUs to facilitate accurate and time ly reporting of health 
sector allocations. With the enhanced flexibility and institutional structures strengthened at the ground level, fuller utilization of 
allocated outlay is expected in future

III.  INFRASTRUCTURE STRENGTHENING 
Healthcare Units  
Recommendations/Observations  
3.2   The Committee while taking note of progress m ade in strengthening the primary health infrastruct ure after the launch of 
NRHM would like to point out that considerable gap still continues to persist. In this connection, Com mittee’s attention has 
been drawn by Performance Audit of NRHM by CAG (Rep ort No.8 of 2009-10). There was a shortfall of 4398 7 Sub-Centres 
(27%) in 22 States/ UTs, 8613 PHCs (31 %) in 21 Sta tes/ UTs and 4200 CHCs (55%) in 23 States/UTs which  were required to 
be created during the NRHM period (2005-12). Target of creation of 30% of new infrastructure by 2007, i.e. 13196 sub-centres, 
2585 PHCs and 1261 CHCs could not be fulfilled. Acc ording to the CAG Report, as many as 14 States/UTs failed to take any 
initiative for bridging the gap. Out of the target of 43987 sub-centres, 8613 PHCs and 4200 CHCs only 2562 Sub-Centres, 685 
PHCs and 138 CHCs could be set-up. The Committee only hopes that 935 Sub--Centres, 178 PHCs and 67 CHCs reported to be 
under construction during CAG Audit must have been completed and become fully functional by now. The C ommittee would 
like to point out that even as per the target of 20 07, there was a shortfall of 9749 sub-centres, also  1722 PHCs and 1056 CHCs. 
Against this backdrop, bridging the gap of 43987 su b-centres, 8613 PHCs and 4200 CHCs by the end of mi ssion period i.e. 
2012 seems to be an uphill task. The Committee woul d like to point out that the targets set up under N RHM were as per the 
population norms of 2001. The shortfall of infrastructure is bound to increase manifold once 2011 census is over and population 
norms revise. The Committee has also taken note of the fact that only very few states like Assam, Chha ttisgarh, Rajasthan, 
Uttarakhand and Lakshadweep had made an attempt to achieve the target of 2007, while the remaining Sta tes reported nil 
achievement. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department has to pursue vigorously with all the non-performing 
States, otherwise even the basic objective of NRHM of having the minimum required infrastructure would  also remain 
unfulfilled. 
Action Taken  

  While considerable progress has been made from 20 05 to 2009, there is a long way to go in meeting the full requirements 
of infrastructure. A comparison of Primary Health Care Infrastructure and Human Resources in HSCs, PHCs and CHCs is given 
in the Annexure-IV .

IV.  MISSION FLEXIBLE POOL 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.1   Mission Flexible Pool provides for activities  like selection and training of ASHAs, upgradation of CHCs and PHCs to 
First Referral Units and Indian Public Health Stand ards (IPHS), constitution of Rogi Kalyan Samitis an d District Hospital 

Management Committees, Mobile Medical Units, untied  funds for Sub-Centres etc. States have the flexibi lity of utilizing the 
funds as per their priorities for the approved acti vities. The Committee notes that maximum expenditur e (31 %) is towards 
infrastructure upgradation, followed by Untied Funds (24%) and State Innovations (9%). 
Action Taken  
  Matter of record. 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.2   The Committee has been informed that the tota l approved outlay under Mission Flexible Pool for t he Eleventh Five Year 
Plan is Rs.33181.07 crore and the expenditure figur es for 2007-08, 2008-09 and 2009-10 (upto January 2 010) are Rs.3151.64 
crore, Rs.2599.13 crore and Rs.2479.17 crore respectively, totaling Rs.8229.94 crore for the three years taken together. Thus an 
amount of Rs.24951.13 crore (approx.) is still left  to be utilized during the remaining two financial years of the Eleventh Plan. 
However, against the projected demand of Rs.8000.00 crore, plan allocation of Rs.3569.70 crore, has been made in 2010-11. 
Action Taken  
  Matter of record. 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.3   The Committee observes that allocation of Rs. 3567.27 crore for 2009-10 was reduced to Rs.3276.17  crore at the RE 
stage. This cut was imposed by the Ministry of Finance on account of slow pace of expenditure. The Committee is concerned to 
note that as on 31st January, 2010, expenditure reported was only Rs.2479.17 crore. Position was no better during 2008-09 with 
States like U.P., Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Himacha1 Pradesh could utilize less than 50% while Bihar and  Chhattisgarh were 
able to spend only 13% and 17% respectively. Very l ow use of untied funds provided under the Mission F lexible Pool in Bihar 
and delayed transfer of funds to the districts in C hhattisgarh have been cited as the main reason for unsatisfactory performance 
in the two States. 
Action Taken  
  Matter of record. 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.4   The Committee is anguished to note the huge s hortfall in utilization of the budgeted funds and a lso the substantial 
variation between the projected demand for funds an d the sanctioned provisions. The Committee observes  that at a time when 
equitable access to health facilities across the so cial and geographical expanse of the country is the  declared policy of the 
Government, such inefficiencies in utilization of f unds can prove to be a potent deterrent. The Commit tee would like the 
Department to impress upon all concerned including the State Governments the imperative need to review  their existing 
mechanism for assessment of requirement of funds an d take corrective action to overcome the deficienci es in the existing 
system so that the possibility of surrendering unspent/under-utilized funds is obviated.

  The utilization of funds as pointed out earlier h as increased considerably under the Mission Flexibl e Pool. In terms of 
release of funds the Mission Flexible Pool has alwa ys utilized more than 99% of the allocated resource s in the last five years.

Recommendations/Observations

to be finalised by the end of 2008. On being asked regarding the latest State-wise progress made so fa r, the Department has 
informed that though there was a delay initially, n ow States/UTs have shown remarkable improvement for  preparation of 
IDHAP. As on date, 617 districts of the country have already finalised IDHAPs, and teams from NHSRC were sent to backward 
districts to facilitate decentralised planning.

  Matter of record.

March 2010, as many as 12 States/UTs are yet to fur nish the IDHAPs 100 per cent. Goa, D&N Haveli and L akshadweep have

to understand what could be the possible reasons fo r such inordinate delays in the submission of IDHAP s. The Committee 
would like to emphasise that Integrated District He alth Action Plans are the very basis for improving the availability of health 
care facilities in a district. In the absence of a concrete plan of action drawn by the districts, pro per health care facilities for 
people residing in such districts cannot be develop ed optimally. The Committee therefore, impresses up on the Department to 
vigorously pursue this issue with concerned States/UTs to furnish the same as early as possible.

  All districts have now been doing the Districts P lans and teams from the Central Government have bee n visiting the 
districts to facilitate the process.

  The year-wise Approved Outlay (BE) and Expenditur e under the schemes namely Basic Training of ANM/LH V s and

at Training Schools, on account of implementation of 6th Pay Commission Report by the States.

4.14   The Committee is not aware about the reasons  for lack of interest on the part of State Governme nts for creating/ 
strengthening the training schools meant for key He alth functionaries with the support of Central Fund s. The Committee 
strongly feels that it is high time for the Departm ent to make an assessment of this crucial area in c onsultation with all the 
States/ UTs and bring about all round improvement. One must not forget that a fully trained and qualif ied health worker alone 
can handle his job responsibilities effectively.

of the ANM Training Centres, the admission capacity  of students increased from 20 to 40 candidates and  in others from 40 to

V.  RCH FLEXIBLE POOL

5.1   The main objective of RCH Flexible Pool is to  bring about the change in the three critical healt h indicators: Infant 
Mortality Rate (IMR), Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR ) and Total Fertility Rate (TFR) consistent with th e goal of National 
Population Policy 2002, the Tenth and Eleventh Plans and Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). The targets to be achieved 
by the year 2012 are to bring down IMR to less than  30, MMR to less than 100 and TFR to 2.1. Against t his, the achievement 
levels as per latest available studies are: IMR 53 (SRS 2008), MMR 254 (SRS 2004-06) & TFR 2.6 (SRS 20 08). One of the 
most important strategies adopted under the Program me is the freedom given to the States to prepare th eir Annual State and 
District level Project Implementation Plan (PIPs) after assessing their need- based requirements.

  Matter of record.

stated that the main factors for high rate of MMR could be broadly classified as delay in decision-making, delay in reaching the 
hospital and delay in initiating appropriate care. Delay in decision-making takes place mainly due to lack of awareness and 
financial constraints. The Committee was informed t hat to tackle these basic constraints, a number of significant interventions 
have been made so far. Awareness and counseling thr ough ASHAs/ANMs/AWWs, availability of financial ass istance through 
Janani Suraksha Yojana for institutional delivery, and skilled providers for domiciliary birth were ci ted as the main 
interventions. The other problem area coming in the  way of checking MMR was delay in reaching the hosp ital due to lack of 
knowledge about danger signs and availability of tr ansport facilities. Here again, ASHAs/ANMs/ AWW s a re meant to do the 
counseling on danger signs. Transport facilities are being made available through JSY and referral services through Government 
ambulances/ PPP arrangements. Another hindrance not iced was lack of availability of operational facili ty for tracking 
pregnancy and its complications. The Committee was given to understand that these hindrances were bein g tackled by 

upgradation of infrastructure at the district level and multi-skilling of Doctors to overcome shortage of critical specialists. As on 
date, 1024 doctors have been trained in anesthesia skills, 543 doctors trained in obstetric skills and  37,162 Staff nurses/ LHVs/

5.21  The Committee has been informed that currentl y type 3 & type 1 virus was in circulation, limited  mainly to 107 high risk

infrastructure, compromised drinking water supply, inadequate health and routine immunization services , high malnutrition 
rates, and poverty have been cited as the main factors responsible for such a scenario. A multi-pronged strategy is being planned 
which includes cross-cutting activities to minimize  the factors facilitating poliovirus transmission i n these 107 blocks while at 
the same time ensuring the highest possible quality of polio immunization activities.

  Matter of record

Action Taken  
  Matter of record 
Recommendations/Observations  
5.23   The Committee is happy to note that the Depa rtment has been diligently pressing forward with various measures to 
contain the spread of WPV-1 and WPV-3 types, especi ally entrenched in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. The Com mittee hopes that 
the introduction of the bivalent vaccine (P1& P3) d uring 2010 would go a long way in eradicating polio  from the country. 
Though the Department has cited that the absolute numbers of polio cases have been reducing over the years, given the massive 
scale on which the programme is being implemented with NIDs, SNIDs and mop-up rounds reported polio cases have shown no 
significant improvement during the past three years. The Committee would like to reckon here that as per the findings of DLHS 
III (2007-08) survey, the all India figures of polio immunization stand at 66.2% only, with Bihar (53.1 %), UP (44.4%), Madhya 
Pradesh (55.1%), Meghalaya (46.5%), Jharkhand (64.4 %), Rajasthan (63.9%) and most of the NE States per forming less than 
the all India average. Given the above levels of PP I coverage in various States, the Committee would l ike the Department to 
explain us as to how the goal of zero transmission can be achieved at the earliest.  
Action Taken  
  The bivalent vaccine has been introduced in the P ulse Polio Programme in 2010 and has been mainly used in the high risk 
areas of UP and Bihar. The NIDs, SNIDs and mop ups are also being implemented as guided by the epidemi ology of the 
poliovirus in the country. The number of polio cases during the first 19 weeks has declined from 40 cases in 2009 to 21 cases in 
2010 for a similar period during the 2 years.  
  The immunization coverage of 66.2% assessed throu gh DLHS III and mentioned above pertains to the evaluated coverage 
of polio vaccination through routine immunization programme and not through the pulse polio immunization programme (PPI). 
The figures of 53.1 % for Bihar and 44.6% for UP also pertain to the polio vaccination coverage through routine immunization. 

  As a part of the strategy to eradicate polio, mul tiple Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns are being conducted in the 
high risk States in addition to the routine immuniz ation programme. The overall polio vaccination cove rage in UP and Bihar 
during these campaigns is extremely high. Independe nt monitoring of the pulse Polio Programme Immuniza tion (PPI) 
conducted by WHO-NPSP monitors has demonstrated tha t the overall pulse polio coverage in UP and Bihar has been 
maintained above 95% during each of the recent campaigns. 
  The Government is making concerted efforts to fur ther improve pulse polio immunization coverage thro ughout the 
country, especially in the high risk States of UP a nd Bihar with a focus on the 107 high risk blocks a nd the migrant population 
where the risk of a continuation of poliovirus circulation is high. 
  The Government is also making efforts to improve routine immunization across the country with a spec ial focus on the 
States that have low coverage as evaluated through DLHS III. Special intensive efforts to improve rout ine immunization 
coverage are being made in the 107 blocks that are at a high risk of poliovirus circulation by improvi ng the quality of delivery 
and access to services through improvements in micr o plans, training, community mobilization & support ive supervision and 
monitoring.

Recommendations/Observations  
7.1   Tuberculosis is a major public health problem  in India. The country accounts for nearly one-fift h of the global incidence. 
In 2007, out of the global annual incidence of 9.23  million TB cases, 1.96 million were estimated to h ave occurred in India, of 
whom 0.8 million were infectious cases. About two persons die from TB in India every three minutes; 900 people every day and 
almost 3.28 lakh every year. The Committee was info rmed that the Revised National TB Control Programme  (RNTCP) has 
been extended to the entire country in 2006. Till d ate, 11 million T.B. patients have been initiated o n treatment with 2 million 
additional lives saved. 
Action Taken  
  Matter of record 
Recommendations/Observations  
7.2   To tackle HIV/TB co-infection, TB + HIV colla borative activities with NACP, initiated in 2001, h ave been scaled up 
across the country. The Committee notes that intens ified TB/HIV package of services have been started in nine HIV high 
prevalence States (Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Pondicherry and Tamil Nadu) 
in 2008 and has been extended to nine additional States (Delhi, Gujarat, Punjab, Rajasthan, Kerala, Assam, West Bengal, Orissa 
and Chandigarh) in 2009-10 with a vision to cover t he entire nation by 2012. Monitoring of co-infected  patients was started 
from 4th quarter of 2008, and out of a total of 310 47 such cases, 5171 cases were treated with a 75 pe r cent success rate. The 
Committee is happy to note that the Department has been pursuing its concerns diligently to identify a nd provide treatment to 
HIV/TB co-infected patients. 
Action Taken  
  Matter of record 
Recommendations/Observations  

7.3  To control this major health problem of the co untry, Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP ) based on 
internationally recommended strategy of Directly Observed Treatment Short Course (DOTS). The Programme has the objective 
of detecting at least 70% of cases and curing at le ast 85% of sputum positive patients. In order to ad dress the problem of Multi 
Drug Resistance TB (MDR- TB), establishment of a ne twork of 43 accredited Culture and Drug Susceptibil ity Testing 
Laboratories for diagnosis and follow-up of MDR-TB patients across the country was being undertaken in  a phased manner. It 
is planned to roll out services for Drug Resistant Tuberculosis in all State/ UTs by March 2011. 
Action Taken  
  Matter of record

7.4   The Committee observes that the emergence of multi-drug resistant TB has increased the severity and magnitude of the 
problem in terms of cost, longer and difficult trea tment regimen. In this context, the Committee welco mes the initiative of 
establishing a network of 43 Laboratories for diagn osis and follow-up of MDR-TB patients. The Committe e hopes that such

charges, if any, proposed to levied for availing of the facilities therefrom. 
Action Taken  
  The programme is establishing the proposed networ k of 43 laboratories at a site identified by the States with the objective 
of ensuring convenient and equitable access while m atching the expected workload in the particular Sta te. In addition, the 
programme is also accrediting and involving identif ied NGO/Private and Medical College laboratories to  supplement the 
diagnostic capacity and further facilitate ease of access. 
  In order to ensure that the patients do not have to travel long distances to access the laboratory services the programme is 
establishing efficient mechanisms for collection an d transportation of sputum samples from microscopy centres (close to the 
patient’s residence) to these laboratories. 
  The programme is providing the MDR-TB diagnostic and treatment services absolutely free of cost to all the patients.

implications by way of debt or commitment charges and if so, the extent of financial liability involved so far. 
Action Taken  
  The World Bank credit of Rs.756 crores is a typog raphical error. It may be read as Rs.765 crores. 
(a) Rs.765 crore credit from the World Bank has bee n converted into loan currency of credit which is S pecial drawing 
Rights. The SDR value of the credit available to Go vt. of India is SDR 115.700 Million. Out of which t ill date 
disbursement under IDA Credit No. 4228-IN is SDR 56 .608 Million equivalent to Rs.389.55 crore. This in cludes

  DRS Survey Report:  State representative drug resistance surveillance (DRS) surveys have been undertaken in Gujarat 
and Maharashtra in 2005-06 and the results of these  surveys indicate that prevalence of MDR amongst ne w cases is 2.4%. 
(Published data from Gujarat) and 2.7% (Unpublished  data from Maharashtra). The prevalence of MDR amon gst re-treatment 
cases was found to be 14% (Unpublished data from Maharashtra) and 17.4% (Published data from Gujarat).

completed the study and the results are awaited. The Western UP study is underway and is likely to be completed by mid 2010. 
The pilot study for the DRS survey in Orissa has been successfully completed. The main study is yet to be started. 
  Social Assessment Study:  The objective of the study was to understand the s ocial context, cultural practices and social 
institutions within which the project is to be impl emented; understand the health seeking behavior of the marginalized and 
vulnerable sections and through this identify factors, which enhance benefits to the marginalized and vulnerable groups. 
  The study highlights that special attention has t o be paid to the local context and needs of the spe cial groups at the local 
level. Accessibility to services is an issue mostly in tribal areas. Need based, area specific interventions, with the involvement of 
local leader have been identified as the best optio n to cater the needs of the people. Use of local po pular media, local leaders, 
and tribal leaders has been identified in the study . Role and importance of CBOs, NGOs and PRIs has be en highlighted. Study 
also emphasizes need to strengthen public private partnership, more importantly in tribal areas.

for its perusal. The Committee would also like to b e apprised of the progress made towards establishin g video conferencing at 
the remaining sites and strengthening the remaining priority labs.

  It is true that recruitment and training of the r equired manpower under IDSP is proceeding at a positive pace. 
  To expedite the recruitment, Ministry of Health a nd Family Welfare has decided that these recruitmen ts will be 
decentralized and the State Health Societies have b een authorized for filling up the contractual posit ions at the State/District 
level. 
  At present, a total of 359 out of the 400 sites h ave been installed by Indian Space Research Organiz ation (ISRO). The 
remaining 41 sites are yet to be installed. The mai n reasons for non-installation of these sites are n on-readiness of the sites, 
equipments short shipped, equipments lost after delivery. The States have been requested to expedite t he process of making the 
sites ready and restore the lost equipments after d elivery; for equipments short shipped, ISRO has been requested to deliver the 
equipments. 

  Strengthening of Public Health Laboratories:  50 priority district laboratories identified in 35  States/UT are being 
focused for strengthening in the country for labora tory diagnosis of epidemic prone diseases. A referr al laboratory network is 
being established in 9 priority States on a pilot b asis to provide access to diagnostic facilities during outbreaks in the remaining 
districts of the State. Comprehensive guidelines fo r the procurement of equipments for the priority di strict labs have been sent 
to all the States. The process of procurement in 16  States (22 labs) has been completed. Active follow -up action to monitor the 
process of procurement of equipments in the remaini ng identified priority labs is being done through t elephonic conversation, 
video conference and on site visits.

3.18  Status of ANMs at Sub-Centres and PHCs  
  The Committee is also quite disappointed with the  progress made over the past four years regarding f illing up the vacant 
posts of the various healthcare functionaries under  NRHM. The Committee observes that one of the most important objective 
with which the Mission was launched at the outset w as to ensure the availability of the various health care functionaries, i.e.  
ANMs/ MPWs(M) /LHVs/ Lab Technicians, doctors and s pecialists at Sub-Centres, PHCs and CHCs at the rig ht places. 
Realizing that their presence is essential for the smooth functioning of health centres and hence, important for the success of the 
Mission, the Committee has been recommending to the  Department year after year to take up the issue of  non-filling up of the 
vacancies with the States/UTs. However, there seems  to be no significant improvement in the situation.  The Committee feels 
that four years of focused attention, and considerable infusion of funds under NRHM, aimed to create a brigade of healthcare is 

a long enough time for the situation to have improv ed. Neither the flow of funds nor the efforts of th e Department are found 
wanting. The only conclusion the Committee can draw is that required manpower for the Health Centres is simply not available 
in majority of the States. 
Action Taken  
  As the RHS comparison of 2005-09 has indicated th ere has been a substantial increase in health human  resources in the 
primary healthcare system. While acknowledging the gap which still exists, the Ministry would like to place on record that over 
7 lakh community workers and more than 1 lakh health workers have been added to the health system under NRHM. Filling up 
of full human resource gaps require longer time span as simultaneous efforts to increase seats in medi cal and nursing education 
have also to be made. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  It is a fact that considerable manpower has been created under NRHM so far. However, the Committee i s not 
convinced by the contention of the Department that a longer time span is required for filling up of human resource gaps. 
One must not forget that NRHM is mandated to be implemented in a mission mode.

some time as it was mandated to be carried out only  through Non-Governmental Organisations. The Commit tee feels

set under NRHM. The Committee feels distressed that  despite its repeated recommendations, the Departme nt has not 
been able to achieve the desired level of capacity building of ASHAs. The Committee once again urges u pon the

4.31   The Committee can well imagine that there ma y be any number of similar cases in other States al so. In such a 
scenario, the Committee strongly feels that the Min istry needs to undertake a country-wide review abou t functional status of 
MMUs. Thereafter, constant monitoring at regular in tervals has to be carried out so as to ensure the a ccessibility of healthcare 
facilities to the general masses. 
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee notes that this is a classic case of the fact that wisdom dawns on hindsight. The Commit tee 
observes that after so much of funds have been infu sed into a healthcare initiative, the assets so cre ated by allocating 
scarce resources seems to be lying idle and unused in so many of the States across the country. The Co mmittee observes 
that if the Department had acted with prudence and foresight, then such a waste of money could have been avoided. The 
Department has not informed the Committee the actua l number of MMUs functional across the country and as to 
whether how many NGOs/Charitable Hospitals have exp ressed interest to operationalise the MMUs. The Com mittee 
would like the Department to inform it about the latest status in this regard while examining Demands for Grants of the 
forthcoming year. The Committee would also like to be enlightened as to whether any proposal has been firmed up for 
providing more MMUs in the inaccessible districts of the country.

Recommendations/Observations  
5.17   Cold chain maintenance is the most crucial c omponent for effective implementation of the Immuni sation 
Programme. The Committee, however, observes that so  far this has proved to be the weakest link under t he programme. 
Committee’s apprehensions have been confirmed by th e assessment of cold chain maintenance arrangement made under the 
Performance Audit of CAG. As per the CAG Audit, non e of the cold chain equipment was available in any of the 124 test 
checked PHCs in Haryana, Meghalaya, Madhya Pradesh,  Puducherry and West Bengal. Besides, in Bihar, Lak shadweep and 
Uttar Pradesh, 31 to 68 per cent of cold chain equipment was found non-functional. 
Action Taken  
  The vaccines are stored in the temperature betwee n 2-8°C in all levels upto PHCs. The cold chain equ ipment i.e.  fridge 
and/or Ice Line Refrigerator storage are used to ma intain this temperature for the vaccine. The advant age of Ice Line 
Refrigerator is that even in case of electricity fa ilure, it can hold the temperature for 72 hours. No rmally an Ice Line 
Refrigerator would require 8 hrs of power supply pe r day to maintain the requisite temperature. The fr idge does not have such 
long hold over time. The States have been using fri dge or Ice Line Refrigerator for storing vaccine. T he deep freezers are used 
for freezing ice packs which are then used in the vaccine carrier for transportation of the vaccine on a session to session basis to 
outreach session site or to other site where the vaccines are not stored. 
  As per the performance audit of CAG (Report No. 8  of 2009-10) conducted in 2007-08 Para 6.5.5 (Annexure-Xl ) none of 
the cold chain equipment was available in any of th e 124 test checked PHCs in Haryana, Meghalaya, Madh ya Pradesh, 
Puducherry and West Bengal. It seems that these PHCs are functioning as outreach session without having storage facility. The 
audit report has not enclosed the list of these 124 PHCs. 
  Instructions have been issued from time to time t o the State governments to get all the serviceable cold chain equipments 
repaired and ensure that no equipment is kept for more than one month for want of repair. 
COMMENTS  OF  THE  COMMITTEE  
  The Committee is surprised by the response of the D epartment to the concern shown by it on non-availab ility of 
cold chain equipment as pointed out in the CAG Repo rt. The Committee doubts whether any follow-up acti on has been 
initiated by the Department on the findings of CAG Report. The Committee would appreciate if the list of 124 PHCs 
inspected by CAG is obtained from it without any further delay and corrective measures are taken accordingly. 
Recommendations/Observations  

5.18   The Committee is more disturbed by the fact that Government of India budgetary support for main tenance of cold 
chain equipments, supply of spare parts, provision of alternate power supply has proved to be of no av ail. The States have 
simply confirmed their inability to absorb the fund s for envisaged purposes. The Committee is of the v iew that the absence of 
cold chain management has indirectly resulted in adverse impact on the UIP, a high priority area under the Mission.  
Action Taken  
  The Government of India has been providing the bu dgetary support for maintenance of cold chain, supply of spares which 
are being used by the States for repair and mainten ance of the cold chain equipment lying with the Sta te governments. The 
provision for alternate power supply has been made to cover-up the period of electricity failure and e nsuring cold chain 
maintenance. The funds utilized by the various Stat es under this provision are annexed in Annexure-XII . It can be seen that 
most of the States have been utilizing the said funds for maintenance of the cold chain. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee notes, from the information given in Annexure XII, that the utilization of funds by as m any as 
eleven States/ UTs namely, D&N Haveli, Daman & Diu,  Delhi, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Puducher ry, 
Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Ut tarakhand for repair and maintenance of the cold ch ain 
equipments ranges between 1.5% to 37.9% which by any standard cannot be termed satisfactory. The Committee views 
this trend with serious concern as the under-utilis ation of funds could have serious implication on th e proper storage of 
vaccines and the resultant efficacy thereof. The Co mmittee would, therefore, like the Department to ta ke appropriate 
remedial measures in this regard for making the UIP successful.

5.27   The Committee views with serious concern the  high level of pregnant women registered for instit utional delivery 
not opting for the same. This clearly indicates tha t various interventions made under JSY so as to mak e aware the targeted 
population about the positive impact of institutional delivery both on the mother and child have not p roved to be very effective. 
Situation becomes more worrisome by the fact that h igh focus States, where need was the most, have bee n showing such a 
trend. The Committee fails to understand the reasons behind ground level functionaries not monitoring the trimester check-up of 
the registered pregnant women. The Committee would like to point out that the achievement of 47 per ce nt of institutional 
deliveries (DLHS-III 2007-08) from 37 percent (DLHS-I 1998-99) although indicates a slow but steady in crease, however, one 
must not forget that 53 per cent women still contin ue to remain deprived of the benefits of institutio nal deliveries. The 
Committee is of the view that the role of ASHA/ANM under the JSY seems to be limited to payment of cas h incentives only. 
Consistent tracking of expectant mother for antenat al and post-partum check-up and deliveries needed m ore focused attention. 
For this, regular monitoring and surprise inspections need to be included as an essential component of JSY.  
Action Taken  
  Regular IEC is being done by the States through m ass media, inter-personal communication during Vill age Health and 
Nutrition days to promote institutional deliveries.  Regular counselling on the benefits of institution al deliveries among the 
expectant mothers is ensured through a network of A SHAs. In order to improve institutional delivery am ong tribal pregnant 
women, ASHA incentive package of Rs.600/-is being introduced in the notified tribal areas. 
  In order to avoid delayed payment and other irreg ularities in the payment of cash assistance under J SY, if any, several 
steps have been taken which include payment through  cheque and display of the list of beneficiaries al ong with the date of 
disbursement at the health institutions. 
  In addition to HMIS, the Ministry also calls for periodic reports from all the States/UTs on physical and financial progress 
to JSY with prescribed format for close monitoring of the scheme. 
  If any irregularities in the payment of cash ince ntive under JSY are reported to this Ministry, instructions are issued to the 
States to investigate the case and take appropriate  remedial action. Central teams also visit the Stat es from time to time to 
monitor the implementation of JSY and make suggestions for improvement. 
  JSY is monitored through several mechanisms. Some  of the key steps taken are: 
  Health Management Information System (HMIS):  A robust system including comprehensive set of for mats for 
periodic flow of information of both physical and f inancial progress from district to State and then u pto the National Level has 
been introduced. 
  Quality Assurance (QA) Cell:  QA cells have been placed at district and at State  level to monitor and evaluate the 
performance of various strategies including training. 
  Community Monitoring:  Community based monitoring of health services is a  key strategy of National Rural Health 
Mission (NRHM) to ensure that the services reach th ose for whom they are meant. The provision for Moni toring & Planning 
Committees has been made at Primary Health Centre ( PHC), Block, District & State levels and at the lev el of community 
through the involvement of Village Health and Sanitation Committee. 

  Programme Management Units (PMUs):  The State PMUs/ District PMUs have been establishe d at State/District level 
to monitor the performance of the programme in their area through regular field visits, evaluation of data. 
  Evaluation Surveys:  Large scale surveys are also organized namely National Family Health Survey (NFHS) on the lines 
of Demographic and Health Surveys conducted in the other countries, District Level Household Surveys ( DLHS), Facility 
Surveys to assess and evaluate the outcome/impact o f the programmes/interventions from time to time. T he surveys throw data 
at district/State level covering the areas viz. Fam ily Planning, Immunization, Maternal Health & Care,  Infrastructure facilities 
available at various health facilities levels inclu ding trained/skilled manpower( medical & paramedica l) in the country. The 
Survey data also gives information by social groups viz. SC, ST, OBC, others. 
  Regional Evaluation Survey:  RETs are responsible for monitoring and evaluating  the programme implementation of 
Health & Family Welfare services provided to the co mmunity in the country and to check the reliability  of information on 
Family Welfare Programmes. This also includes Sample verification of the selected acceptors of Family Welfare Services. 
  Joint/Common Review Missions:  Regular review missions in partnership with develo pment partners and State 
representatives (JRM/CRM) are organized for review and concurrent evaluation of RCH-II and NRHM progra mme 
respectively. These Missions comprise State briefin gs, field visits and State level debriefings, event ually culminating in State 
reports which are used to assess the progress/bottl enecks in implementation of the programme and thus suggest 
recommendations/further actions to be taken. 
  Pregnancy Tracking:  Government of India has taken a policy decision to get every pregnant woman tracked by name by 
the respective State health machinery for provision of timely ANC, Institutional Delivery, PNC along with Immunization of the 
new born. 
  Maternal Death Review:  The Government of India has taken a policy decisio n to review every Maternal death by an 
expert group both at the health facilities and in t he community. This will be done by the States. The purpose of the review is to 
find the gaps in the service delivery which leads t o Maternal deaths and take corrective action to imp rove the quality of service 
provision. 
  Mother and Child Health Card (MCH):  A joint MCH card of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and Ministry of 
Woman and Child Development (MOWCD) has been launch ed for recording of all the service provisions from  pregnancy to 
growth monitoring of the infants. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee takes due cognition of the efforts ci ted by the Department for promoting institutional d eliveries. 
However, what draws the Committee’s attention is th e fact that the Department has been silent about th e shortcomings 
pointed out by the CAG in its Performance Audit of the NRHM (2009-10). Inspite of the above interventi ons and 
monitoring mechanisms if the loopholes pointed out by CAG persist then the objective of such an important intervention 
like Janani Suraksha Yojana to reduce MMR in the co untry would stand diluted. Involvement of Voluntary  
Organisations/ NGOs working in the field of materna l health should be sought to track the number of be neficiaries 
opting for institutional delivery and the number of  beneficiaries under this programme. Even audit of records of 
payments to the beneficiaries should be handed over  to the independent agency to bring forth greater f inancial 
accountability into the programme. In order to incr ease institutional deliveries the Department should  first identify the 
district in a State with very high MMR and thereaft er, should carry out a campaign to track down pregn ant women in 
the area and counsel and persuade them to avail the benefits of the programme. This would be a beginning which can be 
replicated in other areas/districts/ states by givi ng credibility to the service guarantees envisaged to be provided to the 
needy pregnant women under the programme and the resultant outcome, i.e., reduction in the MMR.

Recommendations/Observations  
6.3  The Committee notes that against an allocation  of Rs.442.00 crore in 2009-10, expenditure reported as on 28.02.2010 was 
only Rs.278.61 crore. The Committee observes that t his trend of under-utilisation of allocated fund is  also there in the first two 
years of the Eleventh Plan. Against the provision o f Rs.399.50 crore and Rs.472.25 crore in 2007-08 an d 2008-09, expenditure 
was only Rs.383.66 crore and RS.299.38 crore respectively. The Committee is constrained to observe that against the total Plan 
outlay of Rs. 3190.00 crore for the Eleventh Plan, less than half of the funds were released and that too remained under-utilised. 
Committee’s repeated attempts for optimum utilization of allocated funds under NVBDCP has failed to make any impact. 
Action Taken  
  The allocation is made on Annual Plan basis and n ot Five Year Plan basis. During the year 2009-10, a n outlay of 
Rs.442.00 crores was approved for NVBDCP. On the basis of actual expenditure incurred and likely to be incurred upto March, 
2010, the final estimates to the tune of RS.371.19 crores was approved. The expenditure upto 31.03.2010 is RS.338.87 crores. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee does understand that the allocation i s made on Annual Plan basis but the fact remains th at the 
Department has chosen to remain silent on the issue of underutilisation of funds. The Committee would like to point out 
that total Plan outlay in respect of any scheme is based on the specific requirements, both existing and anticipated. Ideal 
position is to go for optimum and judicious utilisation of allocated funds with the objective of earmarked funds being put 
to use as per the envisaged physical targets. The C ommittee, accordingly, urges upon the Department to  take urgent 
remedial steps to address the issue to ward off any negative impact on the programme. 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.4   The Committee has always been responsive to t he genuine demands of the Department. The Committee would, however, 
also like the Department to focus on better utilization of the scarce resources. The Committee, once again, recommends that the 
Department need to focus on analyzing the reasons f or reduced utilization of the allocated funds and t ake corrective action 
accordingly. The Committee would also like to know whether any commitment charges are to be paid by th e Department in 
case of shortfall in utilization of EAP component and if so, the charges paid during the last three years. 
Action Taken  
  The reasons for reduced utilization of the alloca ted funds are under: 
/circle6 Delayed and incomplete recruitment of human resource under project and contractual staff. 

/circle6 Delayed procurement of goods and services due to a dministrative procedures and stringent guidelines of donor 
agencies. 
/circle6 Poor utilization of the cash allocation made to th e States due to delayed/non-performance of earmarked activities. 
  The efforts are being made through regular intera ction, review and monitoring activities. at regular basis and extension of 
technical support to needy States.  
  As far as NVBDCP is concerned, no such commitment  charges are to be paid for shortfall in utilizatio n of assistance 
provided under World Bank and Global Fund Supported projects currently being implemented.  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee notes that though the Department has identified three clear reasons for reduced utilizat ion of the 
allocated fund under this head, its reply lacks cla rity inasmuch as it fails to indicate substantive m easures taken to 
overcome the problem. The Committee would, however,  like to be apprised about the outcome of the remed ial action 
taken by it to address this issue.

KALA-AZAR 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.13   The Committee observes that though the Natio nal Health Policy (2002) had set the goal of elimination of Kala-azar 
by 2010, the above target is yet to be realized. This is evident from the fact that 2534 reported cases of Kala-azar from the States 
of Bihar, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh have been r eported during the first two months of the year 201 0. It is in this context 
that two rounds of door-to-door search, which were to be undertaken for elimination of Kala-azar, assu me added significance. 
However, the Committee fails to understand as to why Kala-azar fortnights could not be observed in the most endemic States of 
Bihar and Jharkhand during the past year. Inspite o f the Committee’s repeated comments on carrying on intensive door-to-door 

surveillance and monitoring by the Department, the situation so far has been far from encouraging. The  Committee would like 
to be enlightened about the reasons behind not unde rtaking the door-to-door search in Bihar, Uttar Pra desh. The Committee 
recommends that effective surveillance, timely trea tment and compliance of treatment regimens in all P HCs in the affected 
districts need to be continued without any let-up.  
Action Taken  
Kala-azar fortnight was introduced to strengthen th e active case surveillance, which involves 15 days extensive search from 
house to house for the early detection of kala-azar  cases as per case definition of suspected case def initions. A large number of 
persons are required by the States to undertake thi s exercise. Due to the inadequate infra-structure a t the grassroot level, the 
States are not able to observe KA fortnight. States are reminded for strengthening surveillance and in this regard 919 contractual 
Male MPW s are allocated during 2010-11 to State of Bihar to be deployed in 16 high Kala-azar endemic districts. 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.14   The Committee would like the Department to a pprise it in clear terms the number of PHCs in the endemic districts 
that have been provided with anti-Kala-azar drugs, the number of household/ population covered distric t-wise under the door-
to-door surveillance activities, and the physical o utcomes of such initiatives. The Committee would al so like to be apprised 
about the number of NGOs/FBOs/PRIs involved in Kala -azar elimination activities in the above States, t he funds provided to 
them during the last three years, the cases treated  by them and the initiatives taken by them to ensur e treatment compliance of 
the patients. 
Action Taken  
/circle6  Anti Kala-azar drugs are available in all the 523  PRCs in 52 districts of 4 states namely Bihar, Jha rkhand, West Bengal 
and Uttar Pradesh. 
/circle6  Approx. 130 million population is at risk of Kala -azar, which requires door to door active case sear ch for the suspected 
kala-azar cases to ensure early diagnosis and complete treatment. 
  Presently no NGO/FBO/PRI is involved in Kala-azar  elimination activities. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  Kala-azar had remained a serious problem for the co untry for quite some time. The Department has repli ed in its 
ATN that no NGO/FBO/PRI is involved in Kala-azar el imination activities. The Committee feels that the proper 
incentives, support and counseling to the above ent ities would guarantee their involvement in the elim ination of the 
Kala-azar. The Committee fully agrees that for unde rtaking extensive search from house to house, a lar ge number of 
persons are required. Hence, it suggests that the P RIs could be used to be an effective mechanism of a ugmenting 
manpower for door to door searching and case detection. Hence, the Department should devise means of involving PRIs 
in Kala-azar elimination activities. The Committee suggests that the Department should also explore po ssibility of 
involving/ contracting out such activities to the p rivate entities. The Committee hopes that the Kala- azar rounds must 
have been carried out during 2010. The Committee would like to be apprised about the latest status in this regard. 
JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.18   The Committee is dismayed to note that more than four years have elapsed since the vaccination programme was 
launched in 2006, yet the all India coverage of JE vaccination campaign is only 46.62% uptill 2009 as against the targeted 85% 
coverage. What is more worrisome is that JE vaccina tion coverage in four districts of Andhra Pradesh, one district of Assam 
and two districts of Tamil Nadu is nil, which paints a very grim picture, especially in the context of there being no specific anti-
viral drug for JE. The Committee feels that if such  gaps are not addressed immediately, efforts to con tain JE outbreaks will 
stand jeopardized. The Committee, therefore, recomm ends that the Department should, in coordination wi th the State 
Government concerned, chalk out an action plan to a chieve the targeted coverage of JE vaccination and also apprise the 

Committee of the progress made in this regard. Similar efforts for vaccine coverage of the affected di stricts of Andhra Pradesh, 
Assam and Tamil Nadu are also required. 
Action Taken  
  At the time of the submission of the earlier repl y, JE vaccination was underway in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Goa and 
West Bengal, however the process of vaccination in 30 districts in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Assam , Bihar, Goa, Haryana, 
Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Uttar P radesh and West Bengal has been completed except di strict Adilabad in 
Andhra Pradesh where the campaign was to be halted due to bad logistic planning by the State health au thorities. The overall 
percentage coverage of 60.68% has been achieved dur ing 2009. The shortfall in desired achieving percen tage coverage of 85% 
is on account of temporary hold up of vaccination campaign in district Adilabad, poor vaccination coverage in two districts each 
in Goa and West Bengal where the campaign was not launched in accordance with Government of India guidelines and also due 
to the report of 6 Adverse Effect Following Immuniz ation (AEFI) cases in two districts of West Bengal namely Hooghly and 
Howrah. Annexure-XIII . 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee is not convinced by the Department’s reply that apart from Adilabad district in Andhra P radesh 
and two districts of Goa and West Bengal each, the vaccination coverage has been satisfactory. The Committee observes 
that in three out of four districts (i.e. Latur-27. 61 %, Gadchiroli-l1.85%, Washim-52.61%) in the stat e of Maharashtra 
and even in the districts of Krishna, Nellore and Medak of Andhra Pradesh the coverage has been far from satisfactory.

apprised about the latest coverage status for all t he 30 districts where the vaccination was carried o ut and whether a 
follow-up round has been carried out by the Centre to determine the actual coverage of the targeted beneficiaries.

liquidated within a justifiable timeline. The Commi ttee also observes some serious deviations involvin g huge amounts 
from the prescribed financial norms made by some un its in recent times. The Committee feels the Depart ment needs to 
further strengthen its Internal Audit Wing and make  it an effective tool of removing outstanding audit  paras. Proper 
training to staff placed at Units may be one of the  interventions in this regard. The Department, apar t from issuing 
necessary routine instructions, may initiate invoki ng penal provisions in cases of serious deviation. The Committee 
would like to be apprised of the action taken by the Department in this regard. (Para 2.18)  
III.  CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS) 
  The Committee in its earlier report had appreciat ed Department’s initiative of introducing a pilot p roject for 
Preventive Health Check-up for pensioners and servi ng employees over the age of 40 years at CGHS dispe nsaries, 
Sector-12 and Sector-4, R.K. Puram, New Delhi. As i nformed a good number of beneficiaries have benefit ted from this 
facility since its introduction on 24th February, 2 010. However, contrary to Committee’s recommendatio n, the 
Department is non-committal on either the extension  of the duration of the pilot project or extending the project to the 
areas covered by other wellness centres. The Commit tee would like to reiterate its earlier stand that in view of the 
increased lifestyle related diseases, the Departmen t needs to expand this initiative to expand its out reach to more 
beneficiaries.    (Para 3.6)  
  The Committee, while making the observation in pa ra 3.7 had expected the Department to apprise it of  the 
updated status of the proposal regarding forwarding  the Bill for treatment of pensioner CGHS beneficia ries to UTI- 
TSL for payment within 10 days .The Committee, ther efore, once again recommends to be enlightened abou t the 
progress made in the matter. (Para 3.7)  
  The Action Taken Note furnished by the Department  has proved beyond doubt the apprehensions of the 
Committee that the Government wants to dilute its s ocial obligation towards its employees. The justifi cation by the 
Department that the proposed health insurance schem e is primarily aimed at Central Government pensione rs residing 
in the areas not covered by the CGHS and also for t he serving Central Government employees presently not covered by 
the CGHS, does not hold ground as it would be manda tory for the new entrants in Government service and  those 
retiring subsequent to its introduction. Further, t he justification that the capping is a well thought  out exercise and 
would be more than adequate to cover the health needs of the beneficiaries is not convincing at all. To prove its point the 
Department has even stated that a provision for the  creation of corpus for reimbursement of expenditur e beyond the 
annual limit of Rs.5.00 lakhs, on a case to case ba sis, is also a part of the scheme. The Committee fi nds this very 
intriguing that when it is ready to shell out reimb ursement over and above this limit, why the limit h as been prescribed 
at all for the beneficiaries. It is understandable that the Department needs to place a capping while negotiating with an 
insurance agency, but keeping discretion of Departm ent to reimburse amount over and above this amount on a case to 
case basis dilutes the responsibility of the Depart ment and can lead to favouritism or even corruption . Another major 
concern is that whether the Insurance agency with w hich the Government is proposing to reach a tie up would promote 
cashless facilities with beneficiaries. The Committ ee has serious apprehensions about the adequacy of this scheme. The 
Committee, accordingly, outrightly rejects the forc ed enforcement of the proposed Insurance Scheme to Government 
servants and recommends to the Department to concen trate on strengthening this well structured CGHS sc heme and 
continue to fulfil Government’s social obligation towards its employees.  (Para 3.9)  

  The Committee has been advocating the idea of CGH S being transformed into a truly service oriented v enture of 
the Department. However, to its dismay, the Committ ee is finding it very discouraging on the part of t he Department 
not taking it in the right spirit and that too when  it is for its own set of employees. The Committee fully shares the 
concerns of the Department regarding shortage of do ctors. The Department needs to be receptive to the idea, which is 
apparently lacking. The Committee would like to poi nt out that when the double shift system was operat ional, morning 
and evening shift timings were having lesser hours.  With the switch-over to double shift system, the p resent duty hours 
would be accordingly adjusted. The question of havi ng substantial additional staff would, therefore, n ot arise. 
Therefore-, the Committee would again recommend to the Department to improve upon the work culture acc ording to 
the need of the time and move forward in this regard.  (Para 3.11)  
  The Committee observes that 13 plots of land in d ifferent localities of NCT of Delhi are under the p ossession of 
CGHS for construction of CGHS Wellness Centres. All  these plots of land are at various stages of appro val. Status 
Report submitted by the Department clearly indicates that construction work is not going to start at any of the centre in 
the near future. The Committee is not aware about s ince when this process started. The Committee can o nly conclude 
with conviction that considerable time has passed a nd no progress worth mentioning is expected. The Co mmittee is 
intrigued with the details made available about Wel lness Centre at Vasant Vihar. It is very strange th at although the 
sanction for the Centre is not there, construction of boundary wall and provision of security at the p remises has been 
duly sanctioned. The Committee apprehends that this particular plot at Vasant Vihar has been lying ear marked for the 
past so many years. The Committee recommends that t he Department should review the position in respect  of all these 
plots of land and expedite the construction process of Wellness Centres.  (Para 3.17)  
  The Committee is happy to note that a decision ha s been taken for keeping the package rates offered to empanelled 
hospitals and diagnostic centres valid for a period  of two years with the option to continue the same for one more year 
with mutual consent. The Committee would like to re iterate that for life-threatening diseases like can cer, specialized 
hospitals are the best option for patients. In the Capital where the maximum number of CGHS beneficiar ies are 
residing, facilities available at Hospitals like Ra jiv Gandhi Cancer Hospital and Dharamshila Cancer H ospital not 
reaching them due to their remaining outside CGHS empanelment cannot be ignored and needs due consideration of the 
Department. The Committee would, therefore, like to  emphasize that feasibility of such specialized hos pitals under 
CGHS may be explored. (Para 3.28)  
  The Committee appreciates the number of initiativ es taken by the Department for effective functionin g of CGHS. 
The Committee however, feels that wide publicity th rough local and print media needs to be given in th is regard. Only 
then CGHS beneficiaries will be in a position to avail of such facilities.  (Para 3.30)

  The Committee has been constantly monitoring the issue of vacancies in AIIMS, particularly the vacan cies at the

  The Committee is very surprised by the response o f the Department on a very pertinent issue. It is v ery strange

connectivity. The Committee strongly feels that whe n an international organization like WHO can conduc t an

  Status of vacancy position in CHS cadre has been engaging the attention of the Committee for conside rable time.

months. The Committee is constrained to note that e ven this long-drawn exercise has failed to achieve the desired 
results. During 2009-10 against 186 Teaching Posts under CHS cadre 107 Posts were advertised by UPSC a nd only 22

remain very discouraging with the result that publi c at large as well as CGHS beneficiaries will conti nue to remain 

deprived of medical facilities. The Committee is of  the view that the nodal Ministry has to play a pro -active role by 
taking up the issue with UPSC for expediting the re cruitment process as well as analyzing the factors responsible for 
such a low level of joining by successful candidates.  (Para 19.4 & 19.5)
