indicates that all these proposed ventures are at t he initial stage so far as completion of various fo rmalities are 
concerned. Apprehensions made by the Committee last  year about their progress stand confirmed. The Com mittee has 
no other option but to conclude that chances are ve ry dim so far as launching of these programme durin g Twelfth Plan 
Period are concerned. The Committee, therefore, rec ommends that all these new programmes should be mon itored 
vigorously for their initiation at the earliest.  (Para 20.1)  
XXI.   MISCELLANEOUS 
  The ‘National List of Essential Medicine’ intends  to have some noble objective of ensuring abundant availability of 
drugs considered adequate to meet the common contem porary health needs of the general population in th e country. 
The Committee is happy to note that the same is und er consideration of the Department. The Committee r ecommends 
early consideration and clearance of the same by the Department. The Department’s reply is, however, silent on the time 
gap for such exercise. If such a time lag has not b een decided for this exercise of updation of the Li st, the Committee 
would recommend to the Department to work out in-pr inciple time lag for mandatory updation of the List  in future. 
The Committee may be informed about the progress made in this regard.  (Para 21.2)  
  The Committee is aware that the matter is still s ub-judice. However, the Committee recommends to the  
Department to pursue the pending matter in the cour t vigorously so that it does not remain entangled i n prolonged 
litigation and the poor patients are deprived of mu ch needed healthcare needs. The Committee would app reciate if the 
present status of the case is submitted to it alongwith steps taken by the Department to expedite its early resolution. 
        (Para 21.5)  
  The Committee recommends to the Department to ini tiate suitable action to amend the Drugs and Cosmet ics Act 
& Rules so that generic medicines are not allowed t o be sold as branded medicines for the sake of prof iteering. The 
Committee would also recommend to the Department to  ensure availability of generic medicines in the op en market. 
The Committee would like to be informed about the action taken by the Department in this regard.       (Para 21.7)  
  While appreciating a scheme for the healthcare co verage for the deprived sections of the society by the State of 
Rajasthan, the Committee had called for encouraging  such initiatives in different States in all possib le ways including 
extending central funding for the same. The Departm ent’s cold response to this suggestion by terming “ health” as a 
State subject and stating that there was no proposa l for providing central funding for the state-speci fic subjects is 
nothing but outrightly rejecting a good initiative on technical grounds. Had the Department been serio us on this 
suggestion, it would have seized the initiative and started a similar initiative at the Central level whereby all other States 
could be funded from the central pool for undertaking similar initiatives for the poor people.  (Para 21.8)  
(NRHM) 
II.  BUDGETARY PROVISIONS 

  The Committee notes that the cumulative expenditu re figures for the above three programmes, as given  in 
Annexure-I of the ATN, show a promising trend of increase. Yet it is also a fact that the expenditure figures for Routine 
Immunization Programme for the year 2008-09 are too  dismal to be ignored. Large sums of money have bee n left 
unspent under Routine Immunization Programme during 2008-09. The Committee fails to understand as to why a mere 
27.08% of funds could be utilized under Routine Immunization Programme during 2008-09. 
  The Committee is disappointed to note that instea d of apprising it of a specific action plan to chec k the under-
utilisation of funds, the Department has made a gen eric statement that all out efforts are being made to increase the 
absorptive capacity of States where the utilization  is less than the allocation. The. Committee, there fore, suggests that 
the Department should assess the reasons for its failure in monitoring the funds utilisation under these programmes and 
devise means to remove the loopholes, to ensure optimum utilization of funds.  (Para 2.1)  
  The Committee is happy that the Department is pur suing the matter of delay in civil works with the S tates. 
However, the Committee notes that the reply of the Department is silent about the measures taken to ti de over the 
shortage of trained and qualified manpower for prop er monitoring and the lack of infrastructural facil ities. The 
Committee would expect the Department to be more circumspect while furnishing the action taken note in future. 
        (Para 2.13)  
III.  INFRASTUCTURE STRENGTHENING 
  The Committee feels that the Department is very c asual in its reply to a situation of serious concer n. The CAG 
Report findings about the status of Sub-centres, PHCs and CHCs could have been easily made the basis for initiating the 
required corrective measures. The Committee would appreciate if action is initiated in this direction by the Department 
in close co-ordination with State implementing authorities.  (Para 3.4, 3.5 & 3.6)  
  The Committee notes that as per the figures shown  by the Department, there seems to be no significant increase in 
health care infrastructure and the numbers of perso nnel within a span of 5 years. As per the informati on furnished 
above, between 2005 and 2009, the net increase in t he number of sub-centre is 352 only. The number of PHCs 
functioning from Government buildings has increased by 4213 only. The number of Pharmacists posted at PHC/ CHCs 
by 3295 and Radiographers at CHCs by 549 only. Comm ittee’s specific observation about acute shortage o f specialists 
required to be posted at CHCs has elicited no respo nse from the Department. The Committee observes tha t if the 
present requirements and the personnel posted are matched up to the in-position figures, the deficienc ies would be even 
more glaring. The Committee takes due cognition of the fact that creating a brigade of health care personnel is no doubt 
a time taking process, but it observes that 5 year' s time is sufficient to bring about a visible chang e in their numbers. 
The Committee suggests that Mission Directors should be impressed upon to take up with the States on u rgent basis the 
issue of recruitment and posting of personnel as well as bridging the shortfall in infrastructure to meet the targets set up 
under NRHM within a reasonable time frame. The Comm ittee would like to be kept apprised of the specifi c steps taken 
by the Department to overcome the shortage of health functionaries, and for strengthening the infrastructure.  
           (Para 3.17)  
  It is a fact that considerable manpower has been created under NRHM so far. However, the Committee i s not 
convinced by the contention of the Department that a longer time span is required for filling up of human resource gaps. 
One must not forget that NRHM is mandated to be implemented in a mission mode.  (Para 3.18)  
IV.  MISSION  FLEXIBLE  POOL 
  While the Committee appreciates the fact that the  Department intends to make more efforts to upgrade  greater 
number of PHCs into 24x7, it would like the Departm ent to move in this direction in a structured way. The Committee 
would, therefore, like the Department to formulate a concrete and time-bound action plan for upgrading  all PHCs into 
24x7. The Committee does understand the major const raints in achieving the said objective of human res ource and 
physical infrastructure. Accordingly, the Committee impresses upon the Department to address these two basic issues on 
war footing.     (Para 4.6)  

  The Committee observes that upgradation of CHCs t o Indian Public Health Standards is an important 
intervention under NRHM, designed to provide assure d quality health services to the people. Upgradatio n work of 
CHCs in States/ UTs like Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jhark hand, Himachal Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, D&N Haveli,  
Chandigarh, Lakshadweep and Delhi were yet to be st arted at the beginning of the year. However, the De partment has 
not furnished any information as to why such an imp ortant initiative has been set on the backfoot. The  Committee feels 
that the reply given by the Department is generic i n nature and gives no idea of the specific and conc rete action being 
taken or contemplated to be taken to meet the targe t of upgradation of CHCs to IPHS. With only two yea rs of the 
Mission period being left, the action plan regardin g accreditation of the CHCs should have been starte d earlier. The 
Committee, therefore, urges upon the Department to indicate the specific efforts made by it to speed u p the pace of 
upgradation of physical infrastructure. The Committ ee observes that the Department should abandon the lackadaisical 
attitude in the matter and come up with a specific plan to get the CHCs accredited at the earliest and  urges the 
Department to come up with a more elaborate reply in the matter.  (Para 4.7 & 4.8)  
  While making the above observation, the Committee  had expected the Department to initiate some corre ctive 
measures so that greater transparency is ensured in  the functioning of Rogi Kalyan Samitis. The Commit tee, therefore, 
urges the Department to take urgent corrective meas ures in this regard and keep the Committee apprised  of the results 
achieved.        (Para 4.11 & 4.12)  
  The Committee takes notes of the submission of th e Department that the roll-out of the fifth module has taken 
some time as it was mandated to be carried out only  through Non-Governmental Organisations. The Commit tee feels 
that delay in the roll out of the fifth module is indicative of the shortcomings in the coordination mechanism between the 
Department and the State Governments. The Committee  also feels that these issues should have been addr essed in the 
project conceptualization stage itself. The trainin g of ASHAs is an imminent necessity for accomplishm ent of the goals 
set under NRHM. The Committee feels distressed that  despite its repeated recommendations, the Departme nt has not 
been able to achieve the desired level of capacity building of ASHAs. The Committee once again urges u pon the 
Department to immediately initiate appropriate corr ective measures to complete the fifth module of tra ining of ASHAs 
in all the States.     (Para 4.18)  
  From a perusal of the data furnished in the Annex ure VI and VII, the Committee notes that by May, 20 10, the 
second-module training of ASHAs could not be comple ted in Tamil Nadu and Chandigarh, the third module could not 
be completed in Himachal Pradesh. In case of Punjab , Kerala, Haryana, West Bengal and Maharashtra the story is no 
different. The Committee fails to understand the re asons behind such. a poor display of achievements b y the above 
States/ UTs. The Committee finds that there is larg e disparity in the distribution of drug kit among t he States 
irrespective of the number of training module compl eted by them. In case of Bihar, while 49 per cent o f ASHAs 
completed training in fourth module no drug kit has  been issued to any of them. Whereas in Himachal Pr adesh while 
only 36 ASHAs out of a total of 2393 selected could complete first module drug kits had been provided to all the selected 
ASHAs. The case of West Bengal, Gujarat, Haryana, P unjab, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra seems to be no di fferent 
with regard to the disparity in the completion of t raining modules of ASHAs and distribution of drug k its to them. The 
Committee observes that there seems to be no set pr actice being followed regarding distribution of dru g kits and the 
level of training of ASHAs. The Committee would lik e the Department to clarify the reasons for such un even 
implementation of this initiative across the country. The Department should make all out efforts to pr ovide drug kits to 
all trained ASHAs.    (Para 4.21)  
  The Committee is not happy with the vague and eva sive reply given by the Department to its specific observations/ 
recommendations pertaining to the most crucial functionary of NRHM. The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
action initiated by the Department on its specific suggestion to provide ASHA as remuneration a minimu m amount per 
month as allowance as was recommended by the Missio n Steering Group. The Committee would like to be ap prised of 
the findings of the National Health System Resource Centre (NHSRC) Report at the earliest.         (Para 4.24 & 4.25)  
  The Committee notes that this is a classic case o f the fact that wisdom dawns on hindsight. The Comm ittee 
observes that after so much of funds have been infu sed into a health care initiative, the assets so cr eated by allocating 
scarce resources seems to be lying idle and unused in so many of the States across the country. The Co mmittee observes 

that if the Department had acted with prudence and foresight, then such a waste of money could have been avoided. The 
Department has not informed the Committee the actua l number of MMUs functional across the country and as to 
whether how many NGOs/Charitable Hospitals have exp ressed interest to operationalise the MMUs. The Com mittee 
would like the Department to inform it about the latest status in this regard while examining Demands for Grants of the 
forthcoming year. The Committee would also like to be enlightened as to whether any proposal has been firmed up for 
providing more MMUs in the inaccessible districts of the country.      (Para 4.29, 4.30 & 4.31)  
V.  RCH FLEXIBLE POOL 
  The Committee is happy to note that in some of th e crucial states like J&K (DLHS-2-32.0- DLHS-3-63.0 ), 
Uttarakhand (DLHS2-44.5 - DLHS3-63.3), West Bengal (DLHS2-50.3- DLHS3-75.8), Sikkim (DLHS2-52.7 - DLHS -3-
77.9), Daman & Diu (DLHS2-56.1 - DLHS-3-83.5), Raja sthan (DLHS-2-23.0-DLHS-3-50.00), Assam (DLHS-2-16. 0-
DLHS-3-51.00), Bihar (DLHS-2-20.7-DLHS-3-41.4) ther e has been significant improvement in immunization coverage. 
However, the Committee is not aware whether there i s any mechanism for surprise inspections so as to a ssess the exact 
position at the ground level. The Committee would a ppreciate if an initiative is taken for cross-check ing the data 
furnished by these States. Committee’s attention ha s also been drawn by the downward trend noticed in the 
immunization coverage in States like Tamil Nadu (DLHS2-91.4 - DLHS-3-81.6) and Maharashtra (DLHS2-70.9 - DLHS-
3-69.3). The Committee also notes with serious conc ern only marginal increase in the immunization cove rage in States 
like UP(DLHS2-25.8 -DLHS-3-31.1), Madhya Pradesh (D LHS2-30.4 - DLHS-3-38.5), Tripura (DLHS2-32.6 - DLH S-3-
38.5), Gujarat (DLHS2-54.0 - DLHS-3-55.5), Haryana (DLHS2-59.1 - DLHS-3-61.8) and Kerala (DLHS2-78.5- DLHS-3-
79.0). The Committee is of the view that Immunizati on Programme needs to be vigorously pursued in Stat es like UP, 
Madhya Pradesh, Tripura, Meghalaya, Arunachal Prade sh, Bihar, Manipur, Rajasthan where coverage remain s below 
the national average.    (Para 5.16)  
  The Committee is surprised by the response of the  Department to the concern shown by it on non-avail ability of 
cold chain equipment as pointed out in the CAG Repo rt. The Committee doubts whether any follow-up acti on has been 
initiated by the Department on the findings of CAG Report. The Committee would appreciate if the list of 124 PHCs 
inspected by CAG is obtained from it without any fu rther delay and corrective measures are taken accor dingly. 
        (Para 5.17)  
  The Committee notes, from the information given i n Annexure XII, that the utilization of funds by as  many as 
eleven States/UTs namely, D&N Haveli, Daman & Diu, Delhi, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Puducherr y, 
Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Ut tarakhand for repair and maintenance of the cold ch ain 
equipments ranges between 1.5% to 37.9% which by any standard cannot be termed satisfactory. The Committee views 
this trend with serious concern as the under-utilis ation of funds could have serious implication on th e proper storage of 
vaccines and the resultant efficacy thereof. The Co mmittee would, therefore, like the Department to ta ke appropriate 
remedial measures in this regard for making the UIP successful.  (Para 5.18)  
  The Committee takes due cognition of the efforts cited by the Department for promoting institutional  deliveries. 
However, what draws the Committee’s attention is th e fact that the Department has been silent about th e shortcomings 
pointed out by the CAG in its Performance Audit of the NRHM (2009-10). Inspite of the above interventi ons and 
monitoring mechanisms if the loopholes pointed out by CAG persist then the objective of such an important intervention 
like Janani Suraksha Yojana to reduce MMR in the co untry would stand diluted. Involvement of Voluntary  
Organisations/NGOs working in the field of maternal  health should be sought to track the number of ben eficiaries 
opting for institutional delivery and the number of  beneficiaries under this programme. Even audit of records of 
payments to the beneficiaries should be handed over  to the independent agency to bring forth greater f inancial 
accountability into the programme. In order to incr ease institutional deliveries the Department should  first identify the 
district in a State with very high MMR and thereaft er, should carry out a campaign to track down pregn ant women in 
the area and counsel and persuade them to avail the benefits of the programme. This would be a beginning which can be 
replicated in other areas/districts/states by givin g credibility to the service guarantees envisaged t o be provided to the 
needy pregnant women under the programme and the resultant outcome, i.e., reduction in the MMR.  
                 (Para 5.26 & 5.27)  

  The Committee observes that the Evaluation Study of JSY being conducted by the National Health Syste ms 
Resource Centre is yet to start as only required fo rmalities have been completed so far. The Committee  would like to 
emphasize that this Evaluation Study needs to be co mpleted at the earliest so that problem areas can b e identified and 
corrective action taken accordingly.  (Para 5.28)  
VI.   NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAM ME (NVBDCP) 
  The Committee does understand that the allocation  is made on Annual Plan basis but the fact remains that the 
Department has chosen to remain silent on the issue of underutilisation of funds. The Committee would like to point out 
that total Plan outlay in respect of any scheme is based on the specific requirements, both existing and anticipated. Ideal 
position is to go for optimum and judicious utilisation of allocated funds with the objective of earmarked funds being put 
to use as per the envisaged physical targets. The C ommittee, accordingly, urges upon the Department to  take urgent 
remedial steps to address the issue to ward off any negative impact on the programme.  (Para 6.3)  
  The Committee notes that though the Department ha s identified three clear reasons for reduced utiliz ation of the 
allocated fund under this head, its reply lacks cla rity inasmuch as it fails to indicate substantive m easures taken to 
overcome the problem. The Committee would, however,  like to be apprised about the outcome of the remed ial action 
taken by it to address this issue.  (Para 6.4)  
  The Committee observes that there is considerable  gap with regard to District Malaria Officers in tw o N-E States, 
i.e. Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. Out of 16 districts of Arunachal Pradesh, District Malaria Officer is posted in only 3 
districts. Similarly, only 13 districts out of tota l 27 districts of Assam have DMOs. The Committee wo uld appreciate if 
concerted efforts are made by the Department in pursuing this crucial issue with both these two states. 
  Another pressing issue that the Committee would l ike to place on record is that since most of the tr ibal areas are 
highly endemic with Malaria, the outreach of effect ive door to door surveillance services needs to be strengthened and 
carried out diligently. In order to ensure this, th e Committee recommends that the Department devise a  mechanism to 
carry out a monthly review of the surveillance carried out at the district level and to visit specific tribal pockets in order 
to gain first-hand information of the ground realities.  (Para 6.9)  
KALA-AZAR 
  Kala-azar had remained a serious problem for the country for quite some time. The Department has rep lied in its 
ATN that no NGO/ FBO/ PRI is involved in Kala-azar elimination activities. The Committee feels that th e proper 
incentives, support and counseling to the above ent ities would guarantee their involvement in the elim ination of the 
Kala-azar. The Committee fully agrees that for unde rtaking extensive search from house to house, a lar ge number of 
persons are required. Hence, it suggests that the P RIs could be used to be an effective mechanism of a ugmenting 
manpower for door to door searching and case detection. Hence, the Department should devise means of involving PRIs 
in Kala-azar elimination activities. The Committee suggests that the Department should also explore po ssibility of 
involving! contracting out such activities to the p rivate entities. The Committee hopes that the Kala- azar rounds must 
have been carried out during 2010. The Committee would like to be apprised about the latest status in this regard. 
       (Para 6.13 & 6.14)  
JAP ANESE ENCEPHALITIS 
  The Committee is not convinced by the Department’ s reply that apart from Adilabad district in Andhra  Pradesh 
and two districts of Goa and West Bengal each, the vaccination coverage has been satisfactory. The Committee observes 
that in three out of four districts (i.e. Latur-27. 61 %, Gadchiroli-ll.85%, Washim-52.61%) in the stat e of Maharashtra 
and even in the districts of Krishna, Nellore and Medak of Andhra Pradesh the coverage has been far from satisfactory. 
As a result thereof overall 37% of children targeted in AP and 31% children in Maharashtra could be va ccinated in the 
districts given in Annexure-XIII. Even in the State  capital of Trivandrum in Kerala the coverage was o nly 40%. The 
Committee feels that the district programme officer s had perhaps failed to grasp the guidelines of the  Centre in regard 
to this disease. The Committee observes that the re asons for such a communication gap should be ascert ained by the 
Department and appropriate measures be taken to avo id such instances in future. The Committee would li ke to be 

apprised about the latest coverage status for all t he 30 districts where the vaccination was carried o ut and whether a 
follow-up round has been ca,rried out by the Centre to determine the actual coverage of the targeted beneficiaries. 
        (Para 6.18)  
VII.   NATIONAL TB CONTROL PROGRAMME 
  From a perusal of Annexure-XV of the ATN furnishe d by the Department, the Committee finds that, for the 
period April to December, 2009, in 9 States/ UTs no expenditure has been reported by the States TB Societies on account 
of disbursement of funds to NGOs under revised Nati onal TB Control Programme. Again, in another 10 Sta tes/ UTs, 
there is a disbursement of less than Rs. 1 lakh. Th e Committee finds an uneven pattern of funds disbur sement and fails 
to understand the reasons behind such a scenario. I t is also not clear as to whether the lack of disbu rsement is on 
account of less number of VOs/ NGOs functioning in the area or due to lack of timely disbursement of funds on the part 
of the States for the above programme. The Committe e suggests that the Department should come up with a clear 
picture in this regard.    (Para 7.8)  
VIII.  NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME 
  The Committee is astonished by the Department’s r eply that it plans to review the matter of under-ut ilization of 
funds in an emphatic manner with the State Programm e Officers during quarterly and annual NLEP review meetings. 
From the above statement of the Department, it is c lear that there are no proper mechanisms in place t o monitor the 
funds utilization under this programme. The Committ ee would like to state that unless proper monitorin g of the 
programme is done, such lapses would continue and w ith only two years of the Mission period remaining such a trend 
does not augur well for the health of the programme. Hence it exhorts the Department to roll-out financial monitoring of 
the various schemes under the Programme so that the creases are ironed out from the beginning.  (Para 8.8)  
  The Committee observes that out of total 2856 Rec onstructive surgeries conducted on leprosy affected  persons in 
different states during 2009-10, maximum beneficiar ies are reported to be in Andhra Pradesh (617), Bih ar (94), 
Chhattisgarh (108), Gujarat (110), Karnataka (113),  MP (282), Maharashtra (451), Orissa (259), Tamil N adu (132), UP 
(376), West Bengal (101) and Delhi (132). However, as per the details furnished by the Department only  121 persons 
belonging to BPL family could avail of the incentiv e of Rs. 5000/- with 100 beneficiaries being in Kar nataka alone. This 
clearly shows that States have not been fully sensitized about this specific benefits available for leprosy patients going for 
reconstructive surgery. The Committee would like to  reiterate that all the States having higher concen tration of such 
cases need to be sensitized.   (Para 8.10)  
IX.   NATIONAL TRACHOMA AND BLINDNESS CONTROL PROGR AMME 
  The Committee observes that to ensure utilization  of funds allocated for the earmarked activities, i t is essential 
that the remedial measures identified during an ass essment of a programme be implemented at the earlie st so that 
initiatives can be brought back on to the track. The Committee finds that the Department has only passed instructions to 
the States for better financial management and the fact that it has not pursued the matter further is evident from its 
reply. The Committee suggests that with a number of  important entities like Chartered Accountant, MBAs  etc. finding 
place under the NRHM, the State Programme Management Units should be persuaded to execute the remedial measures 
so that the targets under such an important program me are achieved within a reasonable time-frame. The  Committee, 
therefore, suggests the Department to get the feedb ack from the States and formulate further remedial measures if the 
progress is below par.    (Para 9.4 & 9.5)  
  The Committee would like to be apprised of the cl arification sought from the States in this regard.  (Para 9.7)  
  The Committee feels that merely issuing routine i nstructions to the States to ensure standards of Ey e Banking to 
improve utilization of collected eyes is unlikely t o bear fruit. The Committee would expect the Depart ment to devise 
innovative means and methods to objectively assess the progress and analyse in detail the reasons for the shortfall for 
formulating appropriate remedial measures.  (Para 9.10)  

  The Department has merely furnished the figures p ertaining to Tamil Nadu and Gujarat and not comment ed on 
the reasons for low level of utilization of collect ed corneas. The Committee would have appreciated if  the Department 
had dwelt upon the reasons for low utilization and worked out remedial measures to smoothen the inadeq uacies within 
the existing arrangements and storage of the cornea s to bridge out the vast gap between the eyes donat ed and those 
utilized.      (Para 9.11)  
  The Committee understands that the two major reas ons cited for non-utilization of donated corneas ar e beyond 
the control of the eye banks but the third reason c ited in the matter could be addressed to by the Dep artment by 
development of required infrastructure. The Committ ee, accordingly, impresses upon the Department to t ake adequate 
steps to ensure optimum utilization of collected corneas.  (Para 9.13)  
X.   NATIONAL IODINE DEFICIENCY DISORDERS CONTROL P ROGRAMME 
  From a perusal of the above mentioned Annexure, t he Committee is perturbed to find that out of the 
districts surveyed for iodine deficiency, a large number were found endemic. The Committee would like the Department 
to chalk out an action plan to deal with the situation and apprise the Committee about its outcome.  
                  (Para 10.5 & 10.6)

  This Report of the Comptroller and Auditor Genera l of India for the year ended March, 2008 containing the results of the 
Performance Audit of the implemention of the "Natio nal Rural Health Mission" has been prepared for sub mission to the 
President of India under Article-151 of the Constitution. 
  The Performance Audit was conducted between April , 2008 and December, 2008 through test check of rec ord of the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare State and Dis tric Health Societies and health centres covering t he period 2005-06 to 
2007-08. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Annexure-XI (Continued)  
  To support the immunisation programme, cold chain  mainetance was visualised in all CHCs and PHCs. Ou t of 220 
audited CHCs, the essential equipment to maintain c old chain i.e.  ice lined freezers, refrigerators and deep freezer s were 
available in 205 CHCs (93 per cent), 156 CHCs (71 p er cent) and 209 CHCs (95 per cent respectively in 21 States/UTs (details 
in Annex 6.8-A). In none of the 12 sample test checked CHCs in Bihar, was cold chain equipment available. 
  While out of 217 PHCs test checked, ice lined fre ezers, refrigerators, and deep freezers were availa ble in 110 PHCs (51 
per cent), 90 PHCs (41 per cent) and 104 PHCs (48 p er cent) respectively (details in Annex 6.8-B). How ever, none of the cold 
chain equipment was available in any of the 124 tes t checked PHCs in Haryana, Meghalaya, Madhya Prades h, Puducherry and 
West Bengal (5 States/UTs). 

  Further, the equipment available was not put to e fficient use for want of continious power supply an d due to non-
functioning non-availability of standby power sourecs. Besides, in Bihar, Lakshadweep and Uttar Prades h, 31 to 60 per cent of 
cold chain equipment was non functional. 
  The Ministry stated that GOI provided budgetary s upport for maintenance of cold chain equipment to t he States/UTs 
under Strengthening of Routine Immunization as well as supplied spare parts. Further, in case of disruption of power supply, the 
GOI also provided for POL for generator for PHC/CHC  for alternate power supply which can be used for m aintance of cold 
chain. 
  However, it appears that SHSs were not utilizing the resources provided by the Ministry effectively.  The absance of cold 
chain management could adversely impact on the effe ctiveness of the Universal Immunization Programme, a high priority area 
under the Mission. 
  Each Sub Centre under the NRHM was to be run by t wo Auxiliary Nursing Midwives (ANM, female) and a Multipurpose 
worker (MPW, male). The Mission aimed to ensure two  ANMs at 30 per cent Sub Centres by 2007 and 60 per  cent by 2008 
with the second ANM being appointed on a contract b asis . While the ANMs were to be paid out of centra l grants, the MPWs 
were to be paid by the state Government. Among samp le units, 116 sub Sub Centres (9 per cent) of 20 St ates/UTs were 
functioning without an ANM. At 992 Sub Centres (77 per cent) of 29 States/UTs two ANMs were not posted  and in Himachal 
Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Meghal aya, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal  and 
Lakshadweep none of Sub Centres had two ANMs. The deployment of MPWs was inadequate and 775 Sub Centres (60 per cent 
of 27 States/UTs had no MPW. In Bihar, Uttar Prades h, Lakshadweep, Chandigarh and Puducherry none of t he test checked 
Sub Centres had an MPW. In contrast, in Meghalaya, Mizoram, Sikkim and Daman & Diu all the tested sub Centres  had an 
MPW. The State-wise status of non-availability of required staff at Sub Center is detailed in Annex 6.9.

38 th  Report on the ‘Major issues concerning the three v accine producing PSUs,

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Over the past couple of years, the Department-relat ed Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Health and Family Welfare has been pursuing the various issues connected 
with the suspension of manufacturing license of the  three vaccine producing PSUs, 
namely, the Central Research Institute (CRI), Kasau li, the Pasteur Institute of India (PII), 
Coonoor, and the BCG Vaccine Laboratory (BCGVL), Ch ennai; the problems ailing 
them, their revival; effect of closure of the vacci ne manufacturing PSUs on the 
implementation of the Universal Immunisation Progra mme in the country; resultant 
vaccine security in the country etc.,. Since then, the Committee has given three reports on 
the above-related subject, namely, the 34 th  Report on the ‘Functioning of the three 
vaccine producing PSUs, namely, the Central Researc h Institute (CRI), Kasauli, the 
Pasteur Institute of India (PII), Coonoor, and the BCG Vaccine Laboratory (BCGVL) 
Chennai presented to the Parliament on 18 th  February 2009, the 38 th  Report on the ‘Major 
issues concerning the three vaccine producing PSUs,  namely the Central Research 
Institute (CRI), Kasauli, the Pasteur Institute of India (PII), Coonoor, and the BCG 
Vaccine Laboratory (BCGVL), Chennai presented to th e Parliament on the 18 th  
December, 2009 and the 43 rd  Report on the action taken by the Department of He alth and 
Family Welfare on the recommendations/observations contained in its  38 th  Report of the 
Committee presented to the Parliament on 4 th  August 2010.  
 
These Reports were based on extensive and in-depth analysis done by the 
Committee in the light of inputs received from the Ministry, interaction with the then 
Secretaries from the Department of Health and Family Welfare and all concerned officers 
including the DGHS and the DCGI.  
 
The Committee was happy to note that the Government  had assured in the 
Presidential address to  both Houses of the Parliam ent, and at different fora from time to 
time, that  it would make every effort to ensure th at these three vaccine producing PSUs 
are revived and made cGMP compliant. As a sequel to  this commitment, the Department 
appointed a three-member Committee under the Chairm anship of Shri Javid Chowdhury, 

former Health Secretary, on the 25 th  September, 2009 to examine the ‘reasons for 
suspension of manufacturing licenses from the histo rical, technological, 
administrative/organizational and other perspective s’ of the three PSUs, the roadmap for 
their revival and their future role and submit its report within three months. The 
Committee submitted its Interim Report on the 5 th  February, 2010. A perusal of the said 
Interim Report revealed that the fact-finding Commi ttee’s conclusions were in 
consonance with the inferences drawn by this Commit tee, as reflected in its various 
reports. The conclusions drawn by the four-member E xpert Committee (including two 
technical members having expertise in the product/ manufacturing standards of drugs and 
pharmaceuticals), emphatically established that the  decision to suspend the 
manufacturing licence of the premier vaccine-produc ing institutes was not only ill-
advised but also led to acute shortage of vaccines,  - the most essential component of 
Universal Immunisation Programme. It may also be me ntioned that the fact-finding 
Committee has submitted to the Ministry its Final Report on the 10 th  September, 2010.  
 
It was on 26 th  February, 2010 that the Government ordered revocat ion of 
suspension of the licenses of these Institutes. Aft er finding from a perusal of the Action 
Taken Note on its 38 th  Report received from the Department of Health and Family 
Welfare that a number of important issues still rem ained unanswered or the replies 
furnished by the Department were unsatisfactory, th e Committee presented the 43 rd  
Report on the action taken by the Department of Hea lth and Family Welfare on the 
recommendations/observations contained in its  38 th  Report of the Committee to the 
Parliament on 4 th  August 2010. The Department has submitted to the C ommittee its 
Action Taken Note on the recommendations/observatio ns of the Committee contained in 
the Committee’s  43 rd  Report on the 6 th  December 2010. 
 
The Committee’s comments on some of the issues on w hich the action taken by 
the Government is found wanting and/or require furt her action on the part of the latter 
have been placed in Chapter III of this Report.  
 
 
 
  

 CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH RE PLIES 
OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
II INTEGRATED VACCINE COMPLEX, CHENGALPATTU 
 
VACCINE-PRODUCING PSUs vis-à-vis  VACCINE POLICY 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
 
2.11 The Committee finds that no mention has been m ade about the proposed move to 
formulate a vaccine policy which would be the decid ing factor about the kind of 
production to be carried out at the three units. Th e Committee was given to understand 
that the Secretary, Department of Health Research h ad been requested to organize a 
discussion with all concerned. In the absence of an y response from the Ministry in this 
regard, the Committee can presume that no such disc ussion has taken place so far. The 
Committee would like to point out that with the Int erim Report of the Javid Chowdhary 
Committee establishing beyond doubt the manufacturi ng capacity of the three units, their 
viability i.e. continuing to fulfill the vaccine re quirement of the country has already been 
confirmed. Vaccine policy, as and when formulated, can focus on the policy-related 
issues and not on which units are to be closed down or to start functioning. 
 
Action Taken by the Ministry:          
                           
 Observation has been noted. As directed by the Com mittee, the Department of 
Health Research (DHR)/ Indian Council of Medical Re search (ICMR) will focus only on 
policy related matters pertaining to researchable i ssues and /or research findings about

Action Taken by the Ministry:

on the other hand is an optional certification obtained by a company when they determine 
that the certification is beneficial to their opera tions for building up and maintaining 
appropriate systems.

th  Report in February

IX GENERAL OBSERVATIONS 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
 
9.2 The Committee is inclined to agree with the inf erence drawn by the Javid 
Chowdhary Committee. While inspection per se is a c ommendable course of action 
specially to ensure the quality of products related  to the life of infants, it is also required 
to be followed by the requisite corrective measures . In units under Government control, 
this should become the priority of all concerned. Unfortunately, this did not happen in the 
case of these three units. Track-record of the last  decade is ample proof. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly feels that review and revamping  of our drug regulatory machinery 
should be taken up at a priority level.  
     
 
  
Action Taken by the Ministry: 
 As per Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rule, DCG(I) do es not have licensing & de-
licensing power for all the 10,000 manufacturing un its mentioned in the report. These 
licenses are given by State Drugs Controllers.  
 DCG(I) is the Central License Approving Authority as per Rule 68-A of Drugs 
and Cosmetics Act and Rule for Blood Banks, LVP, Va ccine and sera, r-DNA product 
and notified Medical Devices only. Therefore, he ha s to compulsorily inspect the vaccine 
units and ensure the compliance within the conditions of the license(s).  
 The three PSUs were not inspected in 2001 & 2004 a long with WHO observer 
even though NRA assessment was also conducted in th ese years.   These PSUs were 
inspected as per regular inspection procedures thri ce from 2001 onwards which was also 
done for all the vaccine manufacturing units, witho ut any special emphasis or increased 
frequency of inspection for PSUs.  
 The WHOs NRA assessment programme focuses mainly o n the control of 
regulator (NRA) on vaccine manufacturing activity as per legal provisions, irrespective of 
its status as private or public. The three vaccine producing PSUs were inspected 
alongwith NRA assessment on prior approval from Min istry. Therefore, it is not 
appropriate to conclude that three vaccines produci ng PSUs were given exceptional 
attention & assume or indicate that others were not  (for which DCG(I) is not a licensing 
or central licensing approving authority).  
 The deficiencies pointed out were serious in natur e and were required to be 
complied with by the PSUs as per Drugs and Cosmetic s Act & Rules. However, the 

issuance of show cause notice & suspension of licen se was not a problem because of 
weak or selective drugs regulatory machinery, but b ecause of non upgradation of 
manufacturing unit and practice by PSUs as per law of the land (Drugs and Cosmetics 
Act and Rule) in timely or proactive manner.  
 The review of the drug regulatory machinery was al ready undertaken by 
Mashelkar Committee in year 2003 and the measures f or its revamping were suggested. 
Accordingly, steps are also being undertaken by Cen tral Government, in which, under 
Drugs & Cosmetic Act (a) Penalties for manufacture or sale of spurious, substandard 
drugs are increased up to life imprisonment (b) Var ious offences are made cognizable 
and non bailable; (c) provision of establishment of special courts is included.  
 Central Drug Authority Bill is being introduced wh erein a separate Central Drug 
Authority is being contemplated and a separate chap ter each on control of Medical 
Devices, clinical trials and exports are being intr oduced. Central Government is also 
increasing its infrastructure with respect to offic es, laboratories, manpower, testing 
capabilities etc. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
From a perusal of the submissions made by the Depar tment in its action 
taken note, the two assertions that have caught the  attention of the Committee are 
the perceived gravity of deficiencies pointed out i n the WHO-NRA Inspection 
Report of the three PSUs in terms of the Drugs & Co smetics Act and Rules, and 
invoking of legal provisions for allowing WHO to ex ercise a supervisory authority 
over the Indian NRA. The Committee feels that the t win issues are of vital 
importance and intricately linked. Hence, they are required to be analysed 
objectively before any conclusion can be drawn.  
 
One of the major reasons which had been offered by the Department for 
shutting down the three public-sector vaccine-produ cing PSUs was the issue of de-
recognition of NRA by WHO. The Committee, during th e course of its examination 
of the closure of the vaccine-producing PSUs,  was given the impression on more 
than one occasion that if the National Regulatory A uthority, who is the Drug 
Controller General of India, adopts a dual standard  by imposing certain GMP 
norms on private sector but having a completely non -compliant public sector, he 
would stand de-recognized by the World Health Organ isation (WHO) which is the 

main agency for getting the country’s exports to th e other countries. Consequently, 
this would render the private sector vaccine produc ing units ineligible for listing on 
the WHO’s pre-qualified vendor list. However, it wa s the considered view of the 
Committee then that in the name of exports, GMP com pliance and new technology, 
the entire vaccine market cannot be handed over to the private sector and thereby 
push the nation towards an impending danger of vaccine insecurity. The Committee 
was of the view that such an approach by WHO would be tantamount to 
interferences in the sovereign functioning of India  – a fact unacceptable by any 
standards.  The Javid Chowdhury Committee, which ex amined the issue in greater 
detail, held similar views. Some of its comments re levant to the context of the 
present discussion are placed below: 
 
Para 1.4  In the year 2001 and 2004 inspection was carried o ut 
exclusively by Indian Inspectors authorized by the DCGI.   In the 
year 2001, WHO had asked to be associated with the inspection, but 
permission, was explicitly denied by the Indian Gov ernment.  The 
position then taken by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare was 
that in the course of the inspection, the NRA is di scharging a 
sovereign function in which an international agency cannot become a 
partner.   In year 2004 the WHO was not associated with the 
inspection.  However, in 2007, the WHO asked to be associated and 
the Ministry agreed to the request with the approval of HFM. 
 
Para 3.3  …..The Committee notes that the DCGI’s proposal di d not 
give any reason for departing from the earlier deci sion taken by the 
government in year 2002 to not permit WHO to join t he NRA 
Inspection . ……    
 
Para 4.3  ……..  Repeatedly, emphasis has been focused on the line 
that, if the NRA is derecognized, the private manuf acturers will be 
treated as ineligible for WHO pre-qualification as vendors. The 
risk or damage to public interest resulting from cl osure of the 
public sector units has never been considered : though, on a few 
occasions mention has been made that steps will hav e to be taken to 
secure alternate sources of supplies for vaccines.  In sum, it is the 
view of the Committee that the Ministry (including the DGHS and the 
DCGI) did not carry out an appropriately structured  analysis of the 
sensitive issue under review.  The discharge of the  responsibility of 
due diligence by the Ministry required that the var ious facets of the 
issue be discussed in a simple structured manner so  that pros and 

cons were transparent.  The Committee is of the con sidered view that 
had this been done, the Ministry would not have com e to a decision 
to close the units in an abrupt manner.  
 
Para 4.4.1.2   ……… the advice/information offered by WHO- about 
improvement in product standards and technical proc esses,

immense value. However, in order to maintain a harm onious 
working relationship, it is important to accurately  demarcate the 
boundary between the reach of WHO’s advocacy and th e irreducible 
extent of exercise of sovereign authority by the Indian Government.  It 
is known that the WHO has been offering technical a dvice to the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on GMP- relat ed issues. 
However, no matter how useful WHO’s advice may be, the NRA’s 
sovereign function under statute, of inspecting the  manufacturing 
standards of drugs and pharmaceutical units, cannot  be discharged 
in partnership with an international organisation. Under the Drugs 
and Cosmetics Act and Rules, the DCGI is an apex po int of the 
Indian Regulatory System. This was the position tak en by the 
Government in year 2002 when it denied WHO the perm ission to 
conduct inspections jointly with the NRA……….. It is seen that the 
decision taken by HFM on 10-05-07, to permit WHO in spectors to 
be associated with the NRA inspection, is on an opaque note stating 
that Secretary (HFW) has opined that we should not object to the 
participation of WHO representatives in the NRA ins pection. The 
note does mention that in the past the Ministry had  not agreed to 
this request of WHO. However, there is no analytica l discussion as 
to why we should reverse the earlier position of the government. 
 
 
Para 4.4.1.3  ………. However, the assertion which seems to 
have been made by WHO- that if WHO was not permitted to inspect 
public sector manufacturing units (even if these ha d no intention 
of applying for WHO’s pre-qualified vendor’s list),  this would 
result in the de-recognition of the Indian NRA, and  would 
consequently render the private vaccine units ineli gible for listing 
on WHO’s pre-qualified vendor list –seems to be an arbitrary 
conclusion.    On the basis of what has been mentioned earlier,  it is 
apparent to the Committee that WHO does not exercis e any 
supervisory authority over the Indian NRA.  Hence t he question of 
de-recognition of the Indian NRA cannot arise.  WHO  would 
naturally be entitled to make an independent assess ment of the 
level of cGMP compliance of those manufacturing uni ts that apply 
for pre-qualified vendor-listing with WHO.  Needless to say, the

expressed in the above paragraph had been incorpora ted in the 
interim Report, the issue of de-recognition of the NRA by WHO 
seems to have been dropped, and the Indian supplier s of vaccines 
to international agencies have suffered no disadvantage.  
 
Para 4.4.1.4   The Committee is of the considered view that ther e is 
considerable confusion in the dialogue between the Ministry and the

administrative practice, in the normal course, the Ministry should 
have obtained the position of the WHO on this sensi tive issue in

Para 4.4.1.5  ……… While no one disagreed with this line of action, 
the suggestion was never pursued.   The Committee had also 
recommended in its Interim Report that the Ministry  may consider

Health and Family Welfare and the WHO.  While four of the

been accepted by the government and implemented, th is particular 
recommendation does not seem to have caught the att ention of the

suggest that the Ministry may consider entering int o a candid

4.4.1.7   Despite having arrived at the above posit ion on the 
question of de-recognition, the Committee considers  it necessary to 
address the worst-case scenario, one in which, at s ome distant date 
when even those Indian manufacturers that are compl iant with 
WHO-level GMP norms, are not included in the pre-qu alified list of 
vendors. India has been a growing exporter of drugs/ vaccines under 
internationally-funded relief programmes. Exports o f drugs and 
vaccines from the country under such programme are of a value of 
about Rs. 500 crores annually i.e. US$ 0.1 billion.  Even if we 
hypothetically assume that these exports run the ri sk of being 
discontinued, the impact will be nominal, as the va lues of these 
exports is miniscule compared to the aggregate nati onal export

the Committee, the export earnings foregone, if such an eventuality 
arises, would be insignificant compared to the gain  through 
enhanced vaccine security for the country over the long run.  
 
From the excerpts above, it is abundantly clear tha t the case for suspension of the 
licenses of the three public-sector vaccine-produci ng PSUs, inter alia, rested on a 
major misconception and misinterpretation of certai n unclear signals passed 
through the communication from the office of the WH O. A prudent step that was 
blatantly missed by the Ministry was to determine a t the outset the exact position in 
this regard from the WHO. What is astonishing is the fact that it was not considered 
to be clarified later although the matter surfaced time and again (precisely five 
times in the notes at various levels in the Ministr y).  The Ministry’s decision to 
recommend the closure of the three vaccine-producin g PSUs was not only myopic 
but also exposed the nation to an unacceptable risk in vaccine security, while several 
states reeled under vaccine shortages. As has been discussed in the earlier Reports 
of the Committee, in the absence of supply of vacci nes from the public sector, the 

cost of vaccines in the domestic market appreciated  by 50-70 percent within a span 
of two years from the closure of the three vaccine-producing PSUs.  
 The Committee observes that it is high time that t he role and locus standi  of 
the NRA vis-a-vis the WHO are made clear. In the absence of any clear -cut 
boundary in the matter, it is left to the subjective interpretation of the officials at the 
helm of affairs at any point of time. In the view o f the Committee, such a precarious 
situation leaves ample scope for cases like that of  the three vaccine-producing PSUs 
to re-surface in future.  Hence, it strongly recomm ends that the Ministry, which is 
the prime intermediary between the WHO and the NRA,  should take up the matter 
with the WHO and clarify the position at the earlie st. The Committee would like to 
be apprised about the progress made by the Ministry in this regard. 
  
The other point on which the Committee would like t o focus on is the issue of 
the Department’s treatment of the compliance of GMP  norms by three vaccine-
producing PSUs. From the outset, the Department, wh ile justifying its decision to 
suspend the manufacturing licenses of the PSUs, has  offered that they had failed to 
comply with the GMP norms specified under the Drugs  & Cosmetics Act and Rules 
made thereunder. However, in the wake of the fact t hat the vaccines produced by 
the PSUs conformed to the standards of safety, effi cacy and quality, - a fact which 
was admitted by the then Secretary during the cours e of her deposition before the 
Committee on 26 th  October, 2009, - the Committee has been stressing in its 34 th , 38 th 
and 43 rd  Reports that the decision of the Department to clo se these PSUs on the 
grounds of non-compliance lacked justification. The  Committee is, therefore, 
perturbed to note that the Department, instead of a dmitting the fallacy of the 
decision taken by them earlier, continues to harp o n the lack of compliance of GMP 
norms by the three PSUs in its latest ATN also.  Th e Committee would like to state 
here that its observations regarding the Department ’s unfounded decision to close 
the three PSUs has been upheld by similar findings of the Javid Chowdhury 
Committee which has demolished the very grounds on which the Department’s 
decision in this regard was based. The Committee wo uld like to quote the following 
specific comments from the Final Report of the Javid Chowdhury Committee: -

Recommendations/Observations             
     
 
9.4 The Javid Chowdhury Committee had rightfully co ncluded that it needs to be 
recognized that the sudden-death approach to the im plementation of the GMP standards 
would serve no public purpose; it would only bring about a crisis, as the operations of a 
larger portion of the domestic drug sector would co me to a halt. The above facts clearly 
indicate that so far judicious applicability of Dru gs and Cosmetics Rules has been 
lacking. The case of the three public sector units is a classic example of total lack of 
accountability of all concerned. It is time that a fool-proof mechanism for regulating the 
manufacturing units of all categories- both in the private and public sector, is evolved. 
Simultaneously, review of infrastructure and manpow er of the drug regulatory body also 
needs to be taken on a priority basis.  
 

Action Taken by the Ministry: 
 Sudden death approach is not allowed legally in th e implementation of Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act and Rule including GMP through its in built provisions. The rule 85(1) of 
Drugs & Cosmetics Act requires that, the manufactur er shall be given the opportunity to 
show-cause (detailing the deficiencies) prior to ta king action like suspension or 
cancellation. 
 
 This kind of provisions only has allowed our domes tic drug industry to grow to a 
turnover of Rs. 1 lakh crore per annum in 2010 with out any observable crisis especially 
with respect to this procedure for suspension of licensees. 
 
 The Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules, in itself h as various mechanism like (1) 
Mandatory provision to issue show-cause notice prio r to suspension/cancellation of 
license, (2) Provision of appeal to  the Government   by the aggrieved party to challenge 
the suspension/cancellation and power to the Centra l/State Government to allow or to set 
aside that order. Therefore, there is in- built mec hanism for judicious applicability of 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules. 
 
 The three PSUs have also gone through all these pr ocess of inspection in August, 
2007, issue of the show-cause notice on 14 th  December 2007.  Re-inspection in January, 
2008 and review of reply of PSUs and then suspensio n of license. The Central Govt. had 
revoked the licenses of these units in 2010 under t he provisions of the Drugs and 
Cosmetic Act and Rules made thereunder. 
As per rule, the compliance to essential GMP standa rds for the product quality 
and public health cannot be substituted by anything  else and the fulfillment of the 
requirement has to be done by manufacturer and not by regulator.  It is not appropriate to 
link the non-compliance and serious irregularities in the PSUs to goodness or badness of 
regulatory machinery. 
 
 
 Certainly, it is a time for evolving the foolproof  mechanism for regulating the 
manufacturing units of all categories both in priva te & public sector, without any bias or 
special consideration (for Government or private), keeping safety, efficacy and quality of 
the product . In general sense, it means a strong &  effective drug regulatory mechanism 
acting equally for private or public sector. Review of the infrastructure and man power of 
drugs regulatory body was undertaken by Mashelkar c ommittee in 2003. The committee 
has suggested various measures. Accordingly, steps are also being undertaken by Central 
Government in which under Drugs & Cosmetic Act:- 
 
(a) Penalties for manufacturer or sale of spurious, sub standard drugs have been increased up 
to life imprisonment 
(b) Various offences are made cognizable and non bailable. 
(c) Provision of establishment of special court is included. 
 
 The Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill 2007 prov iding inter alia for 
creation of a Central Drugs Authority and Central L icensing of Drugs was introduced in 
Rajya Sabha on 21st August, 2007. The Bill was refe rred to the Department-related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on the 23 rd  August, 2007 for examination and report. 

The Parliamentary Standing Committee submitted its observation/recommendations in its 
30 th  Report on the Bill on the 21 st  October, 2008, which is under 
examination/consideration in the Ministry. Further, fresh views of State/UT Governments 
have been asked for which are being received. 
 
  The Expert Committee on Drug Regulatory Issues un der the chairmanship of Dr. 
R.A. Mashelkar in its report had concluded that the  existing infrastructure at the Centre 
and States was not adequate to perform the assigned  functions efficiently and speedily. 
The Committee felt that creating another authority would not solve the problem at hand. 
It was essential to strengthen the existing organiz ations to enable them to undertake all 
the functions envisaged for NDA.

IX GENERAL OBSERVATIONS 
 
From a perusal of the submissions made by the Depar tment in its action 
taken note, the two assertions that have caught the  attention of the Committee are 
the perceived gravity of deficiencies pointed out i n the WHO-NRA Inspection 
Report of the three PSUs in terms of the Drugs & Co smetics Act and Rules, and 
invoking of legal provisions for allowing WHO to ex ercise a supervisory authority 
over the Indian NRA. The Committee feels that the t win issues are of vital 
importance and intricately linked. Hence, they are required to be analysed 
objectively before any conclusion can be drawn.  
 

One of the major reasons which had been offered by the Department for 
shutting down the three public-sector vaccine-produ cing PSUs was the issue of de-
recognition of NRA by WHO. The Committee, during th e course of its examination 
of the closure of the vaccine-producing PSUs, was g iven the impression on more 
than one occasion that if the National Regulatory A uthority, who is the Drug 
Controller General of India, adopts a dual standard  by imposing certain GMP 
norms on private sector but having a completely non -compliant public sector, he 
would stand de-recognized by the World Health Organ isation (WHO) which is the 
main agency for getting the country’s exports to th e other countries. Consequently, 
this would render the private sector vaccine produc ing units ineligible for listing on 
the WHO’s pre-qualified vendor list. However, it wa s the considered view of the 
Committee then that in the name of exports, GMP com pliance and new technology, 
the entire vaccine market cannot be handed over to the private sector and thereby 
push the nation towards an impending danger of vaccine insecurity. The Committee 
was of the view that such an approach by WHO would be tantamount to 
interferences in the sovereign functioning of India  – a fact unacceptable by any 
standards.  The Javid Chowdhury Committee, which ex amined the issue in greater 
detail, held similar views. Some of its comments re levant to the context of the 
present discussion are placed below: 
 
Para 1.4  In the year 2001 and 2004 inspection was carried o ut 
exclusively by Indian Inspectors authorized by the DCGI.   In the 
year 2001, WHO had asked to be associated with the inspection, but 
permission, was explicitly denied by the Indian Gov ernment.  The 
position then taken by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare was 
that in the course of the inspection, the NRA is di scharging a 
sovereign function in which an international agency cannot become a 
partner.   In year 2004 the WHO was not associated with the 
inspection.  However, in 2007, the WHO asked to be associated and 
the Ministry agreed to the request with the approval of HFM. 
 
Para 3.3  …..The Committee notes that the DCGI’s proposal di d not 
give any reason for departing from the earlier deci sion taken by the 
government in year 2002 to not permit WHO to join t he NRA 
Inspection . ……    
Para 4.3  ……..  Repeatedly, emphasis has been focused on the line 
that, if the NRA is derecognized, the private manuf acturers will be 
treated as ineligible for WHO pre-qualification as vendors. The 

risk or damage to public interest resulting from cl osure of the 
public sector units has never been considered : though, on a few 
occasions mention has been made that steps will hav e to be taken to 
secure alternate sources of supplies for vaccines.  In sum, it is the 
view of the Committee that the Ministry (including the DGHS and the 
DCGI) did not carry out an appropriately structured  analysis of the 
sensitive issue under review.  The discharge of the  responsibility of 
due diligence by the Ministry required that the var ious facets of the 
issue be discussed in a simple structured manner so  that pros and

However, no matter how useful WHO’s advice may be, the NRA’s

be associated with the NRA inspection, is on an opaque note stating
